subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 13, 1985, consideration of the motion of Mr. Masse that Bill C-20, an Act to Amend the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Canadian Radiotelevision and Telecommunications Commission Act, the Broadcasting Act and the Radio Act.
I must say 1 find it interesting and most gratifying to speak to a Bill initially tabled and introduced in the House of Commons by the Liberal Government in the spring of 1984. The Government at the time and its Minister had worked very hard to promote the development of our communications industry and its specific role in serving Canadians.
Its role is, of course, to promote the development of Canadian culture across the country while considering, and this is very important, Canada's cultural diversity.
On the basis of this experience, the Liberals proposed in Bill C-20 that the Governor in Council have the right to issue certain directives to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. This is in fact repeated by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) in clause 14.1. However, the difference, and there is a vast difference between the former and the present Governments, is that the previous Government had won the confidence of the industry and the CRTC by initiating legislation and bills aimed at expanding communications in Canada. The problem is that today, the Party opposite does not have that expertise in communications, nor does it have the confidence of the communications industry.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is very difficult to win the confidence of the industry when the Government has announced an
unconscionable number of cutbacks, and nothing else. I am thinking of the budgetary cutbacks affecting cultural agencies such as the National Film Board, the CRTC, the National Arts Centre and the Canada Council.
As far as the Canada Council is concerned, the Minister of Communications has decided to close the Council's Atlantic office located in Moncton, New Brunswick. I am sure the Minister must have received, as 1 did, a number of letters from the Conseil de promotion et de diffusion de la culture in New Brunswick, expressing their dissatisfaction. Mr. Speaker, I must explain that this organization regroups 14 associations directly involved in promoting and disseminating culture. 1 would add that our part of the country is relatively sparsely populated and our culture, the Acadian culture, is that of a minority. If we did not have those cultural organizations we would lose contact with other groups in Canada and we would be unable to make our culture known in other parts of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Minister realized that by closing the office in Moncton, he was in fact cutting off artists in Atlantic Canada from those in the rest of the country. If our Atlantic artists are to make a career in the arts, they must go outside the Atlantic provinces and make a name for themselves in the rest of Canada. By closing the Canada Council office, the Minister is compounding the isolation of the Maritimes and their people. Mr. Speaker, if we consider that the key role of the Department of Communications is to promote Canadian culture across the country, let me tell you that the Government is not going in the right direction.
That is not all, however, since the Minister has decided to proceed with further, equally disastrous, cutbacks. For instance, the new Government slashed $7 million off budgets to promote cultural projects. And, of course, they keep chanting: Hurrah for Canadian culture! Next, we will be asking: What Canadian culture? At the rate it is being stifled, we will soon be hard-pressed to maintain our own culture throughout the country.
As a matter of fact, I am afraid I denote a growing trend towards the isolation of the various cultures. This comment is strengthened by the fact that the party in office has pared the budget of the Crown corporation whose original mandate was to upgrade Canadian culture throughout the country. I wonder how the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will be able to live up to its mandate now that its operations have been curtailed by S85 million. One cannot talk about reduced

Most lays-offs involved the main centres, but the fact remains that back home, in the Maritimes, quite a few employees of the Crown corporation lost their job. Need 1 emphasize that reduced staff in administration and especially in programming has a direct impact on the overall operations of the Crown corporation.

In a region such as ours, the Acadian region, it is essential that a corporation such as the CBC be in a position to operate without restraints. First, to us the CBC means a Canadian or national presence but, more than that, it maintains the French fact and the French culture in the Maritimes through its French network, Radio-Canada. We do have other francophone media in the region, Mr. Speaker, but not as many as we would wish. The CBC cutbacks gave rise to immediate reaction from organizations such as the Federation des francophones hors Quebec and Nova Scotia's Federation des Aca-diens. Quite rightly, those associations spoke up against the cutbacks.
People have always praised the CBC for its contribution to cultural minorities. It was Radio-Canada that opened the first francophone TV stations in the Maritimes and, to this day, there are still no private television stations broadcasting French programs in the Maritimes-only Radio-Canada does. Most local programs and productions originate from Radio-Canada.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about consultation. They used to say that there would be no cutbacks without consultation first, but I must point out that again those were empty words.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, still on the issue of consultation, I happen to have here an interesting note about-

The National Director of the Canada Council, Brian Anthony, told reporters that the arts community was never consulted about the budget reductions.

And finally, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about the fact that the party across the floor is still busy making further cutbacks in the field of communications, again without consulting the groups involved. I can only decry this unilateral approach and I am firmly convinced that leaders in the communications industry will never have confidence in a Government which shows so little concern for their industry.

Therese Killens (Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic): Mr. Speaker, I was anxious to speak in the House today because in my riding Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic, we have a very specific problem that concerns the CRTC. About three years ago, a community group came to my office with a community radio project called Radio communautaire du nord de Montreal. In a big city like
Montreal, people who stay home like to hear local news. It is like a local newspaper. In my riding there are four local newspapers, and I know my constituents would rather read these papers than the big Montreal dailies.
With this in mind, I agreed to support the community project I mentioned earlier because it covers about five or six ridings in Montreal North, not just my own. I gave the group a "Canada Works 1983-84" of $17,292. I gave them a "Summer Canada 1984-85" of $6,424. They also received a grant from the Department of the Secretary of State in 1984, for $5,700. 1 also obtained a "Section 38" for the fall of 1984, for $11,000. Mr. Speaker, the point I am trying to make is that it is particularly important to my riding that this project be approved by the CRTC.
Radio communautaire du nord de Montreal has held several neighbourhood meetings. It launched a leadership campaign and received many programming requests. It has concluded its viability study and sent its application to the CRTC. They were ready to submit their brief to the CRTC last fall, but, not surprisingly, considering what happened on September 4 last year, everything was postponed. Last week, I met Mr. Guy Jolicoeur, the project's promoter, who informed me he was very disappointed after receiving a letter from the CRTC advising him that his appointment for submitting his brief had been postponed for one year. This kind of delay is intolerable.
Mr. Speaker, my riding has 10 homes for the elderly, and 12.1 per cent of these people are over 65, while 23.4 per cent are between 45 and 64. I also have disabled people in my riding. Among the 10 per cent that are disabled, many are blind. It is a wellknown fact that people with this kind of disability listen to the radio all day and all evening, since they cannot watch television and few are able to read braille.
When I look at the cuts announced in the paper issued last November by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), I find that $75 million have been taken away from the CBC's communications department; $7.5 million from the cultural agencies; $7 million from cultural projects, and $10 million from the CBC's high technology equipment budget. Finally, and this affects my own community project, $22 million have been taken away from the broadcasting licensing department.
I have attempted to give a concrete example of the frustration and aggravation experienced by a small community which had already given clear indication of its needs. I hope the Government will reconsider its decision, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure quite a number of other small communities across Canada are just as disappointed as I am.
I feel 1 have a responsibility to speak for the handicapped who will be severely affected by Government cutbacks in the communications area.
I was on the task force which considered the needs of the handicapped during the 32nd Parliament. At that time we had
February 14, 1985

hearings in 18 cities all across Canada; we received 600 briefs and produced the "Obstacle" Report, in which we brought forward 130 recommendations. The fourth chapter dealt with information and communications and contained 14 recommendations having to do with the needs of the handicapped in the area of communications.
Mr. Speaker, one out of ten Canadians is handicapped, and that means 2.4 million Canadians. It would be urgent for the Government to develop a national policy on their needs in the area of communications. One of the recommendations was that community radio stations should allocate time for the broadcasting of regional and local news. This is something altogether different from national news.
Recommendation 54 was that the CRTC should develop programs with subtitles, provided of course that a broadcasting permit be obtained within a reasonable time. Licensing would be conditional on the addition of subtitles.
Will the S10 million cutback in the CBC's high technology equipment allocation hinder the development of the new subtitling system? Present day technology now allows cable viewers using a special decoding device to watch information on the screen.
The spokesmen for the handicapped consider that method of communications as being essential to cope with a wide range of needs of the hard of hearing in the area of information and leisure. We should keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that all statistics point to the fact that we will have to serve an aging population in the future, and that means an increasing number of persons with hearing problems, our older people being more numerous. In 1985, the average age is said to be 72 for men and 74 for women.
Another recommendation affecting the daily life of all our people with hearing problems is the prohibitive cost of longdistance calls. Because the method for receiving the message is slow, due to the fact that the message must be typed and received on a small screen, the Government should ask provincial governments and telephone companies as a priority to apply a rate reduction as soon as possible. I must say that Bell Canada has already accepted this, but the country is served by other smaller telephone companies.
I should like to touch on the question of the CBC regional service. In 1977, less than 10 years ago, the CBC was allowed to set up facilities in a city of the Lower St. Lawrence called Rimouski. How surprising! The entire population had to get involved beginning with Mrs. Eva Cote, then president of the Liberal Association and former Member for the constituency of Rimouski. She worked in close co-operation with Jeanne Sauve, then Minister of Communications. Some eight years later, the CJBR station in Rimouski is facing cuts and lay-offs. With 45,000 residents, Rimouski is an important city. Indeed,

it is considered as the economic center of the Lower St. Lawrence.
One has to wonder whether the Government opposite is not moving backwards. I could go on and on but the Speaker is now indicating that I should very soon put an end to my remarks.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to mention that I am concerned about our Canadian artists. They are also affected by this legislation. Without programs such as Les beaux dimanches, there would have been no opportunity to appreciate the works of Marcel Dube, hear Maureen Forester, or see Karen Kain dance. Some people such as Toller Cranston, Louise Marleau, Anne Murray and many others would be known only abroad. Some 20 years ago, all our Quebec artists had to go into exile in France to launch their career. 1 will not speak of Rich Little nor of Paul Anka and all the others who went to the United States to become famous. We are pleased and very proud to say that all those people are Canadians. They belong to our culture. I think that it is a good reason enough to oppose that Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-20 relating to the CRTC. It will do a number of things. In particular, it will give the Government the power to direct the CRTC to implement government policy. As we are living in a very rapidly changing world in telecommunications, especially as it relates to satellite communications, to the changing role of cable television and of direct broadcast, the Government really needs this power.
When we look at many rural areas in the country, we see a situation developing where local television broadcasting stations have a very difficult time being financially successful. Often they are owned by the local cable network which carries 10 or 12 other channels-American ones, other Canadian ones and so on. Naturally the viewers want to watch these channels. Without a cable fee each month to subscribers, the local television station broadcasting off air would have a very difficult time making it financially. We have to have policies, and the Government has to be in the position to make policies so that we can maintain local television stations and ensure that they have the power to raise money through cable systems.
In the outlying areas of the country we see a twin stick operation in many cases, where local television stations carry CBC and CTV network broadcasting; for example, we see that in Sault Ste. Marie and in places like Sudbury. It took a few years for the CRTC to recognize the necessity for the cable and local television broadcasting facilities being tied together.

February 14, 1985
CRTC Act
In a sense we have that situation because without it local television stations could not be viable economically.
Some people would say that carrying CBC, CTV, Global and the other networks does not matter. However, I think it matters for us to have locally produced programs. They increase Canadian content. They give us local information about the area or district which they serve. It is very important for the Government to continue to adopt policies which ensure strong local broadcasting capacities for our stations.
One of the great concerns of many Hon. Members, at least on this side of the House, is just what policies the Government will adopt. In the recent economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), we find serious cut-backs in all manner of the arts. With the new power being provided in this Bill, we have to wonder just what policies the Government will announce. We have already seen the following cut-backs: $75 million in the CBC, $1.5 million in the National Film Board, $1.5 million in the CRTC, $1 million in the NAC, $7.5 million in the Canada Council and $7 million in the communications department.
I am especially conscious of these cut-backs because I had the opportunity to work in the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee last spring on C-24, the Crown Corporations Bill. At that time the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) was the critic for culture and the arts. We heard very strong speeches in favour of the arts and in favour of arm's length activity with the arts. We were able to design that Bill so that in the end the independence of the artistic community and the grants to the Canada Council were maintained. However, we have to worry about the strong statements made during the election campaign with regard to arm's length dealings with the arts and with the strong financial support to the arts when we reconcile them with the speeches of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) here in November and the interviews he has given, as well as the cut-backs which took place in the artistic community announced in the economic statement of early November. For example, in August, in response to a question from the Canadian Conference of the Arts, the PC Government replied:
We are committed to maintaning federal funding for the agencies and councils in line with inflation.
It does not say anything about the $75 million cut-back that came about three months later for the CBC, the cut-backs to the National Film Board and National Arts Centre. We wonder what happened between August, 1984 and November, 1984.
In reply to another questionnaire, the PC Government replied:
We are committed to real growth in federal contributions to this sector.
A few months later we saw massive cut-backs taking place in the artistic community totalling $121 million. In response to
another Canadian Conference of the Arts questionnaire in August, 1984, the Government stated:
Our commitment to improving the quality as well as the quantity of employment in the cultural sector is firm.
After the economic statement of November 8, we found that the CBC was forced to lay off 1,100 people Therefore, we have to wonder whether these commitments mean anything.
We were very impressed with the interventions of the Hon. Member for Rosedale at the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee meetings last year in support of the arts and its independence. How that had changed by November of this year! In an interview with The Globe and Mail on November 29, the Minister of Communications said that he wanted to rethink the arm's length principle and that his Government was moving rapidly to apply direct political hands in the affairs of the CBC.
It is interesting that when the plans were being made for cuts in the CBC of some $75 million, that was not done by the CBC alone. Three outside consultants were hired to decide the fate of the CBC. We are very concerned about where the Government's policy is now compared to before it came to power.
The CBC provides a unique service, not only to the country at large but to various regions. The CBC broadcast out of Sudbury covers all the communities in north-eastern Ontario. Even though those communities are all considered to be in one geographical area, they have very little ties except through the CBC. They receive feeds from the Canadian Press, Broadcast News or whatever, but the CBC is the only organization which ties all of these communities together in a regular CBC radio broadcast mechanism.
I hope the Government will take these concerns into account and develop policies for the future, not undercut and slash the artistic communities and essential services like the CBC as was done in November last.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, Bill C-20 will help us to make things better.
Hon. Members opposite criticize the Progressive Conservative Party for the cut-backs of $75 million at the CBC, but we must point out, and all Canadians should know this, the rationale for these cut-backs was to put an end to the shameful waste of money at the CBC. This is the truth, Mr. Speaker. We should not be afraid to say so.
People today want to defend the artists. I have been a member of the Union des artistes for over 25 years, Mr. Speaker, and I can tell those who want to defend the artists today that these people have been penalized for over 20 years by the CBC. This corporation helps about 40 people. All Canadians watch television! Where are our young musicians? Where are our young dancers? Where are our great Canadian singers? They have to leave Canada to earn a living.
February 14, 1985

They now say that they want to defend the great Canadian culture. Shame on them! Shame on the Members opposite who weakened this great culture for 20 years to help their friends, who have always been the same people. You also watch television, Mr. Speaker. You will agree with me that it resembles a game of musical chairs. The programs may change, but the people remain the same. Our old actors are no longer working, Mr. Speaker. It is always the same guy, who is given a wig and told: You will play this old man. At the same time, our old actors, who have a lot of experience, are completely forgotten. And what about the young musicians coming out of our academies of music, Mr. Speaker? What will they do? They will do what they have been doing for the last 20 years: They will play their instruments in their own kitchens.
Such is the result of the former administration under the Liberal Party.
Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party is in charge now and we want to correct the situation and recognize the true worth of our artists. We also want to give them a chance to really come out and to develop and promote our great Canadian culture in this country. This is the truth, Mr. Speaker. We have seen many strange things in the past. Some people today for the sake of a cause are describing the Progressive Conservative Party as terrible and sleazy because CBC's budget was cut by $75 million. Flowever, the truth must come out. We have no jurisdiction over the CBC. You know that, Mr. Speaker. There is a man at the helm called Mr. Juneau and he is the one who decided to snap off radio antennas across Canada. Fie asked no one for permission. He does not want to follow instructions. He was told to stop wasting money. There are people at the CBC who have been there for 20 years. They have never produced anything and they have five or six people working for them. They are producers who have never produced anything. It is in such instances that we have asked that expenses be trimmed by $75 million.
I can give you another example. At one time, it was decided to produce a program called La course au bonheur at a cost of $1.5 million but this program was never shown. Strangely enough, Mr. Juneau made a statement and said: Well, we were wrong, we made a mistake; it was a miscalculation. We shall try to improve the situation.
Even the Auditor General of Canada has said that CBC had the worst management. This is a fact, and I think that it is important to support legislation such as Bill C-20 to correct the situation and to restore, in the interests of our Canadian artists and all the Canadian people, the true cultural role of the CBC.

I think Mr. Juneau has administered the CBC well and it is thanks to the CBC if some groups are well represented in the French Canadian culture.
In a modern society such as ours, communications are of utmost importance. The impact of a televised broadcast can be assessed. Very positive programs have a positive impact. As evidence of this, I should like to refer to the visit John Paul II paid to Canada. All those who wanted to see the Holy Father were able to do so, just as they were able to see Her Majesty the Queen and witness major events. I will never forget Prince Charles and Lady Diana's televised wedding; it was a major event indeed, the like of which we could only expect to see in movies. Yet, it was for real. The impact of such great events is positive. But disturbing events can have a major impact too. In that context, Mr. Speaker, control over our system of communications becomes all the more important. My colleague who acts as critic for the Liberal Party in the field of communications has already pledged our support for this Bill, but we hope that in future the Government will continue the work already begun by the Liberal Party. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for letting me say a few words at the last minute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications, I rise to support the Minister's overview of Bill C-20. At the outset, I would like to thank Hon. Members on all sides of the House for the quality of debate that has ensued in recent days on second reading of Bill C-20. To the Minister, myself and my colleagues on this side of the House, the contributions made in the debate up to this point in time have been very useful and valuable and will contribute significantly to the committee stage to which I think all Members of the House would like to see this Bill referred as quickly as possible. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this Bill covers and awful lot of ground and there is much detail to be covered in the committee stage as Members assess the impact of Bill C-20.
The Bill proposes to reduce the regulatory burden in communications. It proposes to allow the Government to set policy directions for the CRTC and telecommunications and broadcasting policy while maintaining necessary procedural safeguards.
With regard to the Broadcasting Act, the Bill proposes to create policy objectives that give the CRTC a mandate to deal with abusive programming, and I will return to that in a moment. The Bill proposes to reduce the burden of the broadcasting regulations on the private sector. We in this House have raised a number of questions about Bill C-20. I want to assure the House that at the earliest possible moment we will get this Bill into committee and review all of the questions which have been posed by Hon. Members. In just ten minutes I do not have time to deal with all of them. One feels something like a mosquito in a nudist colony; there is so much ground to cover, one has no idea where to begin.
I will try, Mr. Speaker, to make three quick points on behalf of my Minister. Bill C-20, as I pointed out yesterday to the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), is deeply rooted in the thinking of the previous Liberal administration. That is to say, the Lambert Royal Commission and a special parliamentary committee on regulatory reform became an integral part of the previous Government's broadcasting strategy as it affected directions to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. So in effect we are doing a rerun of our predecessor's policy.
The second point is that it is about time that Parliament dealt with the whole area of sexually abusive broadcasting, indeed, abusive broadcasting of any kind. This matter was the subject of a special subcommittee during the previous Parliament, the result of which was a unanimous all-Party series of recommendations. At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for her passionate dedication to that particu-
February 14, 1985

lar subcommittee. The untiring energy and effort she put into that subcommittee, of which I was the only Conservative Member at the time, will go a long way to making some very important changes in the whole area of abusive programming. This is one area which Bill C-20 intends to deal with head on.
The third thrust, or the theme, which I could suggest to my colleagues is that Bill C-20 is indeed complex in terms of its impact on the CRTC and on the entire broadcasting industry. As a broadcast journalist by profession, I am the first to admit that the nature of this legislation does raise questions as to the role of the Government in terms of what we Canadians can see and hear. We must come to grips with the most fundamental question of all in a free and democratic society. How far is the Government prepared to go in determining what we Canadians can see and hear? Where must Governments stop if our citizens cry interference in their right to watch and hear anything they want?
When people talk "open skies", they mean deregulation and the right to pick out of the air anything they want. How realistic is it, Mr. Speaker, for Parliamentarians to try to regulate the clouds? If "open skies" means the erosion or destruction of the Canadian broadcasting system as we know it, and ultimately a Canadian cultural identity as we treasure it, then where and when does the Government step in? To what extent can or should the Government, this Progressive Conservative Government or any Government, tell Canadians what they should or should not watch or hear?
These are very big questions, Mr. Speaker, and it is up to us as Parliamentarians to try to answer them. We cannot do so in ten minutes here or even in this second reading debate, but again, with luck, when we get Hon. Members and witnesses before the committee on Bill C-20, we will be able to address the concerns about the role of the federal Government in communications policy in that committee.
There are a couple of matters with which I want to deal very quickly in the time remaining. I was impressed by the intervention during the second reading debate by the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) regarding the CBC's treatment of Newfoundland's second oldest radio station, CBG Gander. Both the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate and our colleague on this side of the House, the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson), while remarkably temperate in their remarks, are vigorously supported by their colleagues on the government side. It is a very important matter to the whole of northeastern Newfoundland.
Other Hon. Members have raised comments about the effect of CBC cut-backs on their various areas, but at this time I will only refer to this particular case. I Find the CBG Gander situation to be of real concern when 1 learn that for a savings of $75,000 a year, as the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate pointed out, CBG Gander will be cut off from the people of northeastern Newfoundland. The CBC in the meantime has spent at least $99,500 to redecorate and recarpet the tenth floor of its executive offices on Dorchester Avenue in Montreal. I think those kinds of situations need to be looked at a little more carefully and I intend to raise more fully in
CRTC Act
committee my concerns along those lines. I thank the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate for pointing out this discrepancy.
I would like to deal just briefly with the sexually abusive and abusive broadcasting segment because this is a matter which is dear to my heart. There are some advantages to spending some time on the opposition side of the House because one gets the chance to deal with issues and make strong recommendations in committees and subcommittees. I believe one of the most important issues I have ever dealt with since being elected to Parliament is the question of sexually abusive broadcasting and violence in broadcasting.
I believe this is something that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has to come to grips with in terms of a new broadcasting policy under this Government. I am one of the First to go along with suggestions made by Hon. Members such as the Hon. Member for Broadview-Green-wood, who pointed out that, notwithstanding the provisions of Section 3, we should be talking about the dignity and the quality of all people. It is a good suggestion, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the Hon. Member will raise it before the Standing Committee. I have already drawn it to my Minister's attention.
Again, may I thank Hon. Members on behalf of the Minister of Communications for their worth-while and valuable contributions to this second reading debate on Bill C-20. I believe there is a feeling in the House of Commons now that we would like to see this Bill referred to the Standing Committee as quickly as possible and, Mr. Speaker, I will be there along with my colleagues to deal in a very meaningful and responsive way with the new broadcasting legislation in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commence by thanking the opposition Parties for agreeing to pass this Bill through all stages today. We all agree this Bill will do a great deal for veterans who deserve this kind of treatment, and putting it through today will enable it to become effective very quickly. I know the veterans of this country will appreciate the
attitude expressed by all Members of the House in their willingness to see this Bill pass quickly. I thank the two Members who have spoken on behalf of their Party for their generous and co-operative attitude which has been expressed today.
The proposed legislation, Mr. Speaker, which I have the honour to present to the House contains five amendments to the Pension Act which will be of benefit to veterans and their dependants. The first amendment deals with the annual increase in the basic rate of pension. It has been increased each year by the percentage increase of the Consumer Price Index. This amendment will provide that in future the rate of pension will be increased each year by whichever is greater, the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index or the percentage increase of the average wage of five selected categories of public servants. This change will remedy a situation which for years has been very unfair to veterans because the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index has often lagged behind the percentage increase gained by these public servants. In 1984 this difference amounted to $611. This change will benefit 90,000 pensioners plus 51,000 spouses, children and orphans.
The second amendment will continue a disability pension at the married rate for 12 months following the death of a pensioner. The reduction to the single rate now begins at the end of the month in which the pensioner dies. This change will remove the shock of an immediately reduced income at a time when the spouse is under the emotional stress of such a grievous personal loss. This change is in line with a provision of the War Veterans Allowance Act which has been in place for years. Some 6,000 widows and widowers are expected to benefit from this change. The third amendment will extend the same right to survivors of pensioners who had been receiving attendance and/or exceptional incapacity allowance. Three hundred widows and widowers will benefit from this change which can only be described as very generous.
The fourth amendment deals with the Pension Review Board, the final stop in the pension process and which is currently facing an eight-month backlog of cases. The legislation will provide for the appointment of up to four additional members to the Board. The appointments will be for six months' duration and as required. This provision will guarantee to our veterans and to the Board that the Department will be equipped to meet the challenge of speeding up our examination processes in every possible way.
The fifth amendment will permit pension entitlement boards to be composed of two or three commissioners, as opposed to the present necessity of having three. This should allow these boards to process a third more cases each year. More importantly, this change opens up the whole question of what happens on a split decision. Past practice has been to turn down the veteran's application whenever a split decision occurred. Once the legislation is passed, every split decision will go in favour of the veteran.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud of this legislation. Every amendment is good news for veterans and their families. Almost as
February 14, 1985

importantly, these very long overdue changes have come about within five months of our taking office. They demonstrate the Government's commitment to those who served our country so well, and they demonstrate this Government's determination to help those Canadians who need our assistance.

Mr. Speaker, as the Official Opposition critic for veterans affairs, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-28, a Bill introduced by the responsible Minister and containing amendments to the Pension Act.
Mr. Speaker, first of all I am very glad that the amendments reflect a generous measure of compassion for those who served their country during the last three armed conflicts, in 1914-18, 1939-45 and the Korean War. During these three wars, many Canadians were killed on the battlefield; 66,000 in 1914-18, 44,000 in 1939-45 and 576 during the Korean conflict. They all left behind dependents and families, and many came back physically disabled as a result of wounds received in action.
Perhaps I may recall the words spoken by Sir Winston Churchill in a message to his countrymen during the last war, and I quote:
"Never have so many owed so much to so few".
These words are particularly appropriate today, because that small band of valiant soldiers who defended the principle of freedom so well over the entire world is becoming increasingly smaller today. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am particularly happy with the amendments to the Pension Act made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) for the benefit of those who deserve to receive far more from their country.
The Bill is another in a series of measures brought in to amend the Pension Act, since 1969 and 1970, especially, and continuing, annually, up to 1984. Mr. Speaker, these reforms were made mainly following recommendations by the Woods Report, which I think provided the stimulus for bringing about amendments to the Pension Act with respect to allowances or pensions paid to veterans and their dependents, so much so that it was said, and I quote:
{English}
The years since 1970 have been the most important ones in the history of pension legislation. During this period sweeping changes were made to the Pension Act to provide Canadian veterans and their dependants with benefits that are not exceeded by any other country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, this explains very well that the eight amendments to Bill C-28 complement the work already started with the Woods Report, and also reflect the implementation of some of the recommendations of the Marin Committee. Although that Committee has not been allowed to complete its mandate for reasons of timing, this nonetheless allowed the
Pension Act
Chairman of that Committee, at the express request of the present Minister, to submit a tentative report dealing with 62 major points which Mr. Justice Marin has decided to consider before giving his answers.
Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, part of those answers are included in Bill C-28, and I hope that the other, unresolved questions will be considered more in depth by the Department in order to bring further remedies eventually.
We should keep in mind the work done by the predecessors of the present Minister. One name comes to my mind, that of the former Minister, the Hon. Dan McDonald, who was seriously wounded overseas during the war. His memory is recalled in the Hall of Honour of the federal building named after him to house the Department of Veterans Affairs in Charlottetown. To keep the memory of that worthy son of Prince Edward Island, his battle dress jacket is permanently exhibited. The material on the left side, next to the heart area, was burnt by a stray bullet which went through and glanced off the prayer book he kept in his left breast pocket. This is what saved his life, Mr. Speaker. Mr. McDonald did a lot for war veterans.
Mr. Speaker, if the present Minister of Veterans Affairs has not reached the summit of his excellent political career in other portfolios he held in a distant past on in those he was responsible for a few years ago, he can now boast of having reached it in the position he now holds. I would like to commend him for maintaining continuity in the policy of compassion developed by his predecessors, especially the late Dan McDonald.

Let us take a quick look at the historical background of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I will briefly summarize major developments and legislative changes in veterans' affairs since 1969. Prior to World War I Canada's veterans consisted of a comparatively small number who had fought in the Fenian Raids, the Northwest Rebellion, the Nile expedition in 1885, and the South African War. No particular government agency was formed specifically to take care of the needs of these veterans.
Early in World War I the Canadian Government was asked to move all its seriously wounded soldiers back to this country. In order to satisfy this demand, extensive hospital accommodation and professional and other staff were required. The Military Hospitals Commission was set up by Parliament in 1915 to react to this situation. In 1916 Parliament decided that disabled veterans should be entitled to training for a trade or profession for which they would not be handicapped. The vocational training division was organized to administer this project.
By 1918 the volume of rehabilitation work had increased to the extent that the Department of Soldiers Civil re-establishment was formed to take over the administration of disability pensions, hospital care, training, and placing in employment. Under the Soldiers' Settlement Board many veterans received

February 14, 1985
Pension Act
government loans to establish themselves as farmers in Canada.
As the rehabilitation work lessened it was combined with that of the Department of Health and a new Department of Pensions and National Health was formed in 1928. This Department continued to administer veterans' matters until toward the close of World War II, it became evident that an expanded rehabilitation organization would be required. Consequently, in 1944 the duties of the Department of Pensions and National Health were divided. Those that affected veterans were taken over by a new Department which is the Department of Veterans Affairs.
With regard to pensions, up to June, 1916 all military pensions were administered by the Pension and Claims Board of the Department of Militia and Defence under the Pension Act. In 1919 the responsibility for pensions was given to the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada, then responsible to the Minister of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment. The administration of pensions has remained under that Board, the name of which was changed to the Canadian Pension Commission. Since 1944 the responsible Minister has been the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
Under the 1971 amendments of the Pension Act the Pension Review Board was established to deal with appeals from entitlement and quantum award under the Act. The Board is also authorized to interpret the Pension Act. The 1971 amendments also established the Bureau of Pensions Advocates as a separate organization reporting directly to the Minister. The Bureau is an independent agency established for the sole purpose of providing free legal aid to pension applicants in the preparation and presentation of their claims to the Canadian Pension Commission Entitlement Board and Pension Review Board.
With regard to allowances, the War Veterans Allowance Act was passed in 1930 to provide assistance to Canadian veterans who were suffering economic distress and who, because of the rigours of active service in World War I, were considered to be pre-aged or otherwise permanently unemployable or incapable of self-maintenance. Subsequently the benefits of the Act were extended to others, including veterans of other wars in which Canada had participated, to British and allied veterans, and to widows, orphans, and dependent children, and in 1962, through Part XI of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, to certain categories of civilians who had served in wartime.
The War Veterans Allowance Board was established in 1936 to replace the War Veterans Allowance Committee which had been established in 1930. The Board acts as a court of appeal for applicants and recipients who are grieved by any decision of a military authority.
I will review the major veterans' affairs developments and legislative changes since 1969. In February, 1970 changes were made to the total disability provisions of the group life insurance contract between the director, the Veterans' Land Administration and the Imperial Assurance Company of Canada, permitting a greater number of seriously disabled
veterans to take advantage of the plan. Previously a benefit clause that provided for premiums to be waived in the event of total disability for a period of at least six months had caused underwriters to screen them out of the loan insurance plan. At the above date, the disability benefit was declared optional and many who previously could not obtain coverage could then do so.
In March, 1971, there was a major change that included a 10 per cent increase in disability pensions and a 15 per cent increase in war veterans' allowance rates, and amendments granting special pension status to former prisoners of war of the Japanese.
The new legislation also created, first, the Pension Review Board, an appellant body for the appeals of veterans who are dissatisfied with the decision of an entitlement board; second, the Bureau of Pension Advocates which provides free legal assistance to any applicant or pensioner under the Pension Act.
There were some other amendments as well. In March, 1972 amendments to the war veterans allowance and the civilian war allowance legislation included the exemption as income of cost of living increases of old age security and the guaranteed income supplement.
Again in 1972, cost of living adjustments in pensions and allowances paid to the veterans and their dependants provided for review of pensions and allowances each September and adjustment upward at the beginning of the following year by the increase in the consumer cost of living index during the preceding 12 months.
In February, 1973 amendments to the veterans' treatment regulations doubled travel allowances and accommodation rates for veterans reporting for medical examinations or treatment. In 1973 an amendment to the Pension Act raised the basic rate by 24 per cent and, for the first time, based the basic rate on the average compensate salary of five categories of unskilled employees in the Public Service. The amendment also provided an established relationship between the basic pension and the pension of dependants so that in future years the rates of these dependants will be adjusted in accordance with the established percentages.
In October, 1974 there were other amendments. Previously no allowance was paid for dependent children. The amendment provided for $50 a month for each child less the amount of the family allowance paid on behalf of a child of a widow or widower, or an allowance received and stipulated that the additional allowance paid to an orphan, may be continued to age 25 as long as the child continues his education.
New legislation in 1975 provided equality of status and rights for male and female pensioners. That is, a female pensioner would now be eligible to receive additional pension for husband and children. In 1976 amended legislation provided compensation on a sliding scale tied to the period of time spent as prisoners of war to those who were prisoners of the Germans, Italians and North Koreans. In addition, compensa-
February 14, 1985

tion for those who had been prisoners of war of the Japanese was improved.
Also, on October 28, 1976 approval in principle was given to relocate the Department of Veterans Affairs and related agencies from Ottawa to Charlottetown. It was estimated that the transfer would take four to five years. Agencies and programs to be transferred included the Canadian Pension Commission, the Pension Review Board, the War Veterans Allowance Board, the Bureau of Pensions Advocates and the administration services of the Department.

I know this move has caused much discussion and I wonder today whether history will not be a better judge and acknowledge that such a change, the Department's relocation, has served war veterans and the public service well.

In January, 1977 benefits payable under the Pension Act, War Veterans Allowance Act, Compensation for Former Prisoners of War Act and Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act were increased. Disability, widows and orphans pensions were increased 8.6 per cent in line with the rise in the Consumer Price Index. There were further benefits each year until 1984. It is not necessary to cite all the amendments to improve these benefits for the Canadian veterans.

Mr. Speaker, as Honourable Members will realize, this brief summary reflects a gradual evolution and a constant improvement of the pensions, allowances and services provided to veterans, their wives, their survivors and dependants.
Bill C-28 introduced today will improve even more the living standards of these veterans who are the pride of our nation. The eight amendments it contains are necessary to provide a better service in processing or reviewing applications made by Canadian veterans. All have complained with reason about the prolonged delays caused by the Pension Review Board, which represents the last stage in the pension application process.
To speed up the operation of the Review Board, four new or additional members will be appointed, which should indeed reduce the deplorable delays in the waiting period, that have sometimes reached from eight to ten months.
Another provision of the Bill states that the Entitlement Boards can be made up of two or three members of the Commission, instead of requiring that three be included as is now the case, to bring some flexibility into the process and to simplify the hearing of such cases.
Another amendment would guarantee the same benefits for the survivors of pensioners who received the attendance allowance or the exceptional incapacity allowance or both. It is estimated that 300 widows and a few widowers will benefit from this amendment.
Pension Act
Another important amendment will provide that the invalidity pension at the rate of a married pensioner will be maintained for 12 months after the death of a pensioner. At the present time, the pension is brought down to the rate of a single pensioner one month after the death of the pensioner. I would describe this change as a compassionate amendment, Mr. Speaker, as it will reach 6,000 widows who will certainly find it beneficial.
Mr. Speaker, another very important change, in my opinion, is that a situation which has been quite unfair for veterans for many years will be corrected, as increases were based on the cost of living index. It should be noted that these increases were often lower than those given to the five categories of nonspecialized Federal public servants. The difference for 1984 amounted to $611.
Thanks to these new amendments, the basic pension rate will now be increased automatically each year on the basis of the highest of either the consumer price index or the average wages of the five categories of non-specialized Federal Government workers. Formerly, the basic pension rate was increased automatically on September 30 on the basis of the consumer price index for the last twelve months and the rate was adjusted on the following January 1, as was done this year.
In addition, when a ruling on a veterans' pension application is not unanimous, the benefit of the doubt will be given to the veteran and the ruling of the Board will always be in his favour.
And finally, at present the Canadian Pension Commission is authorized to pay the cost of the attendance of the applicant and his or her witnesses at Entitlement Board hearings. No such provision is provided for attendance at Assessment Board hearings. Bill C-28 will authorize the CPC to pay the cost of attendance at Assessment Board hearings.

In short, Mr. Speaker, that is the scope of Bill C-28. As I said at the outset of my remarks, I would also like to draw the Minister's attention to the health of veterans who were exposed to atomic radiations in the fifties. Apparently, some of them are seriously ill because for years they were exposed to atomic radiations at Chalk River, in the Nevada desert or in the deserts of Australia.
I hope that the Government will accept the request of those veterans who would like to have medical examinations as soon as possible so that, like their colleagues, they will be granted a pension or a disability allowance, should the Canadian Pension Commission so decide.
Before concluding, I would like to mention the beneficial effects of the Aging Veterans Program. It is a dynamic program which enables a good many veterans to continue to enjoy the comfort of a family home instead of being isolated in

February 14, 1985
Pension Act
rest homes. Still on a trial basis, I understand that this program has been highly praised by those who were able to take advantage of it. This is a comprehensive and generous program, and I hope that the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Minister will take every opportunity to publicize this outstanding program which should be readily accessible to all qualified applicants.
If 1 may, Mr. Speaker, I extend my congratulations to all organizations, voluntary or otherwise, and to all people who directly or indirectly have for so many years been advising veterans and looking after their well-being and health. Our veterans rightfully expect a lot from us, but unfortunately we have not always given due consideration to their legitimate claims.

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated earlier today my Party, the New Democratic Party, wishes to see this Bill proceed through all stages as quickly as possible, hopefully one o'clock, and thus have this measure referred to the Senate.
At the outset 1 want to say that I do not want to speak for too long, but 1 do want to take the opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) for bringing forward this legislation. If anything, I think the Minister was a bit too modest in his remarks to the House. I have been around here since 1980 and I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. Various groups, such as the Canadian Veterans Association in Canada, the Canadian Legion and others, have appeared before that committee attempting to impress upon the committee the need for changes in legislation. For the first time since I have been on that committee we have a Minister who has actually met nearly ever major proposal ever presented to that committee.
Hear, hear!

To give you some background into what I meant about the Minister being too modest, Mr. Speaker, some of these proposals have been made to that committee since 1919. One of the major proposals which the Minister has presented to the House concerns the basic rate of pensions, which will finally be increased to reflect parity with the average take-home pay of selected categories of public servants. This proposal was presented in 1972 by a joint Government-veterans' organization committee. It is quite significant that the calculations on this new formula are to be made on the basis of parity as of September 30, 1984, and the adjustment is to be made on the first day of the second month following the month in which Royal Assent is given. This is one of the reasons we are extremely anxious to have this Bill passed through the House today, so that veterans and dependants can receive the increase as soon as possible.
I could talk about the legislation but I think the Minister has adequately expressed to the House its intent and the previous speaker from the Official Opposition has given us a rather lengthy briefing on the history of veterans' pensions and
the legislation affecting veterans over the years. 1 certainly have no intention of repeating much of that.
However, it is incumbent upon me to express some concern. I hope the concern does not last too long. The Minister knows that he will have my full co-operation in attempting to correct some of the real inadequacies in the existing legislation. For example, it completely escapes me why Canadian veterans who served overseas during wars and who subsequently elected, for one reason or another, to remain overseas are denied some aspects of veterans' pensions. They are in fact required under the Pension Act to return to Canada to reside in this country for 12 months. They would then be eligible for veterans' allowances. Many of these veterans of the day are getting older. Many are suffering financial hardship and have families, particularly in the United Kingdom and the United States. These people do not have the financial resources, or their family circumstances do not allow them, to return to Canada for 12 months.
I think that situation is absolutely ridiculous and I know the Minister is concerned about it as well. I would like to see that aspect of the legislation changed. We are not talking about a large number of people or large amounts of money, but those veterans who put their lives on the line for this country deserve better treatment than they have been receiving.
There is also much concern about the Dieppe prisoners of war who in many cases suffered severe hardship as a result of capture in that disastrous raid. These individuals should be given the kind of consideration to which they are entitled.
Most of the serious problems under the legislation are corrected by this measure brought forward by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Many of the problems we have had in the past, and I have no intention of enumerating them at this time, have been administrative problems, attitudes on the part of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and 1 do not mean this unkindly. With the legislation that has been in place there has been a question of how policy was being interpreted and applied to those veterans. Unfortunately, the way it has been applied has created untold suffering for many veterans and their families. 1 am hopeful that the measure before us, which is innovative in my view, will clear up many of these administrative problems.
I notice this legislation states that the Minister will appoint additional commissioners for a six-month period. We will see how that works. The Minister is prepared to review that matter, and if it does not work we will try to do something else to make it work even better.
That concludes my remarks, Mr. Speaker. 1 congratulate the Minister. He knows the Veterans Affairs Committee attempts to work in a non-partisan way. Every member of the Committee is concerned about the interests and worries of our veterans. I hope we will continue to work together in the best interests of all of us.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the Minister, but first of all I thank him for this Bill and I can tell him that we will support it.
Some military personnel were allegedly subjected to radiation during certain tests in Australia, in Chalk River, which is not very far from Ottawa, and in the Nevada desert. I think the Minister mentioned some time ago in a public speech that these people would be examined by medical staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare and, consequently, if it is proven that they suffered injury, they could be covered under the Pension Act. Does the Minister have any intention of bringing in that sort of amendment soon? Perhaps it could be done in committee. Also, will he tell us whether it will be retroactive to January 1, 1985?

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad the Hon. Member asked that question, as I have been working on this matter for quite some time. We have contacted as many of these veterans as we possibly could. We are still trying to contact more of the veterans who were subjected to radiation at Chalk River, in the Nevada desert or in the Australian desert. These veterans are now being examined, by doctors of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The Minister of National Health and Welfare very graciously and generously agreed to do this job for me. These veterans are being examined and, as I have said, if the doctors indicate that any serious illness which these veterans have developed in intervening years could have been caused by their being subjected to radiation, I will recommend very strongly that these veterans be very seriously considered for pensions. I think I can assure the hon. Member that if such a recommendation goes forward, a great deal of attention will be paid to it.

speechtext: I would like the Minister to confirm on Clause 13 that, in the event of a split decision by the commissioners, the decision in favour of the veteran will prevail. Is my understanding correct?

will make it possible without any shadow of a doubt that the benefit of the doubt always goes to the veteran. That is a key part of our new policy. In every case the pensioner must be given the benefit of the doubt.
In my talks with veterans' associations and Members of Parliament who represent pensioners when I took over the portfolio, I received the very definite impression from a great many of those who spoke to me that it appeared that those examining veterans' pension applications seemed to be trying to find ways of not giving the pension to the applicant. I think we all agree that we are dealing with a very special group of people in this country today. Mr. Speaker, in a major speech to his Party's multicultural conference last June, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) outlined five personal priorities for a multicultural policy in Canada. One of these priorities was economic equality and opportunity.
Next month the Government will be hosting a national economic conference at which time participants from all sectors will have an opportunity to share their own economic agendas. Despite many assurances, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the only national body representing ethnocultural communities, has not been invited as a participant. The Council has been asking the Government for months for a seat at this conference. Last year I wrote to the Ministers of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) regarding this very subject and thus far my representations have gone unanswered.
It is time that the Government had the courage and decency to place some much needed action behind its great words of promise. Ethnocultural leaders and organizations are becoming quite agitated at the Government's empty sing-song performance.
The Canadian Ethnocultural Council rightfully deserves to be a participant in this conference and I urge the Government immediately to ensure its involvement and contribution. For the Government to deny the Council this opportunity would be for the Government to ghettoize what is an important Canadian reality.

Mr. Speaker, the hysteria regarding access to abortions should be cooled. It is time the Government supported sound family planning to
prevent unwanted pregnancies, to eliminate the need for making very difficult decisions on the question of abortion, and to provide choices for women.
Planned Parenthood provides information on family planning and on safe contraceptive methods, an issue of growing concern to women. It provides sex education programs and counselling. It helps families as well as individuals. Its aim is to encourage family planning so that children will be wanted and loved, and parents will be able to provide the care that children need. It helps young people to understand their sexuality and the importance of preventing unwanted pregnancies.
Pregnant women can receive the information and help they need to make the choice that is best for them and their families. Teenage mothers may be referred to support groups for schooling and housing, or a young girl may decide not to have a child and may be referred to a doctor to discuss a legal, safe, medical abortion.
We urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to support funding for Planned Parenthood and to encourage research into safe methods of contraception. Unwanted pregnancy should be prevented. Women should not be the victims of street battles.

Mr. Speaker, the Government has an obligation to assure the civilized world that Canada does not harbour war criminals, but the Government also has an obligation not to suggest in its search for war criminals that those Canadians of German descent who fought for their country during World War I and World War II are war criminals. We honour these people as citizens who have done a great deal to develop the strength, character, and expertise of this nation.
Unfortunately, in an effort to try to assure the world that we do not harbour war criminals, it has seemed to some that the Government is out to castigate the German people. This must not be the appearance of what we are doing. World War II has long passed. All wars are a tragedy. Families and persons involved are injured, and bear the scars of those injuries. However, inquiries should not be used to fan racial prejudice, to stir up old hatreds, or to settle old scores.
Old scores should be long buried. This is Canada. This is a new country, and the old scores of the old world do not belong in Canada. While we should look for war criminals, justice is not advanced for any by the revival of memories of torture, injustice, and old bitterness.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill concerns the establishment of the International Centre for Ocean Development, which is commonly known as ICOD. I should like to make a few remarks to clarify this Bill.
We believe that the International Centre for Ocean Development will add an important new dimension to our efforts to assist less fortunate nations. Canada, a great maritime centre, will use this Centre to share its long experience and expertise in marine resource management. As we are all aware, the ocean is a potential major source of food that needs to be developed as soon as possible.
Recently we saw the generosity of all Canadians as manifested in the Ethiopian effort. This, of course, was a short-term action and it is important that we add credibility to our effort by providing long-term solutions in aid of developing and Third World countries. Therefore, we wish to take further initiatives.
Through the efforts of the Canadian International Development Agency, the International Development Research Centre and the many Canadian non-governmental organizations active in the development field, Canada is assisting numerous countries in Africa, Asia, and, closer to home, in Latin America and the Caribbean to improve their standards of living and develop their resources. ICOD will support and further enhance these particular efforts.
February 14, 1985

The abundance of our ocean resources was recognized some time ago and in December, 1982 representatives of 119 nations, including Canada, signed the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Individual nations now lay claim to 40 per cent of the world ocean resources through the 200-mile zones adjoining their coastlines.
I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to provide some background for my proposal today to establish ICOD through legislation in Parliament. At the 1981 Commonwealth meeting in Melbourne, Australia, Canada announced its intention to establish an international centre for ocean development to help Third World nations develop their marine assets, particularly as a source of food. In November of 1983, ICOD was incorporated on the initiative of the Government of the day as a non-governmental organization under Part II of the Canada Corporations Act. Its funding was to come from CIDA. But before making a firm commitment regarding this funding, the present Government reviewed ICOD's mandate and institutional structure. This review led to the conclusion that ICOD could indeed play an important role in helping Canada to achieve its development assistance objectives. However, we are convinced that ICOD's status as a non-governmental organization is not in keeping with its genesis or its source of funding. We believe that, since ICOD was established at the instigation of the Government and is government funded, Parliament should have the right to review its activities, its performance and its budgetary submissions.
I wish to underline, however, that since the funds for ICOD will be taken from the existing foreign aid budget, no additional expenditure will be required. It is a question, rather, of ensuring that ICOD's status is a reflection of reality, that it was created by the Government, and that it relies on the public purse for its Financial support. I would like to note here that this conclusion echoes the recommendations made by the original consultants who were hired to study and evaluate the various operational possibilities with respect to the establishment of ICOD.
The legislation before us makes only minor changes to ICOD's present structure and makes no changes to its objectives.
The affairs of the new centre will be managed by a chairman, a president and 12 other directors appointed by the Governor-in-Council. I would like to point out here that all of the Canadians sitting on the present board of directors have agreed to resign. The Government will appoint 12 new directors and, at the option of the Government, five of these directors can be non-Canadians. This is a tradition which is consistent with other programs. We think it beneficial to have the views of other leaders and representatives of other nations so that they can properly indicate to us the proper course of action so that the programs which we are offering are indeed of assistance to their countries. ICOD will continue to direct its operations from its head office in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Indeed, this may be one of the highlights of this particular piece of legislation as it is further testimony to the expertise
Ocean Development Centre
and momentum of the Maritime Provinces as a whole in the area of marine resources and development.
Why should we establish such a centre, Mr. Speaker? The answer is simple. As a major maritime nation, Canada has established a reputation in the scientific, technical and managerial aspects of ocean management, both in the public and in the private sector. Many Canadian training and research centres have already established links with foreign institutions and international development projects. In establishing ICOD, Canada will take advantage of this experience and its bilingual capacity to provide this urgently required expertise to the Third World. Many international agencies have already responded to ICOD's preliminary contact in a positive manner and have indicated their willingness to work jointly in these endeavours. I am thinking in particular of the United Nations development program, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, and the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Co-operation.
I would like to outline briefly ICOD's specific objectives. ICOD will encourage co-operation between the peoples of Canada and the developing countries in the field of ocean resources development in the following ways: First, by initiating and supporting programs in participating developing countries to improve management and utilization of ocean resources, particularly-but not restricted to-as a source of food. Second, it will encourage the development of indigenous institutions in this field. Third, it will provide training, technical assistance and advisory services. Fourth, it will ensure the distribution of information and sponsor research that is consistent with ICOD's terms of reference. In working toward these objectives, ICOD will draw on all the academic and technological resources of Canada and other countries.
Of course, ICOD will offer programs of assistance in response to the specific national objectives of developing countries but it will, at the same time, encourage a pattern of ocean resource exploitation that makes sense for all. By bringing people from developing countries to undertake practical training in Canada, we will gradually build up a group of professionals who are familiar with Canadian techniques and skills. They will form an international network of experts who have links with Canada, automatically creating new openings for Canadian business to trade with the Third World.
The gap that exists between the ocean's known potential and the present poor rate of return is a clear indication of the need for rational management of these resources. Its initial and most obvious benefits would be the opportunity to supplement food resources and increase employment. Industries such as tourism, energy, marine culture, mining and transportation will also benefit. ICOD will increase Canada's ability to make realistic and innovative proposals in a field whose importance was recognized globally during the negotiations which culminated in the signing of the Convention on the Law of the Sea. This legislation reflects the concerns of Canadians for the future of less favourred nations and reaffirms our Government's intentions of actively assisting in their development.

Ocean Development Centre
