speechtext:
That is one of the things that concerns me about this Bill when the Hon. Member says he is going to appoint a completely new group of directors.
On November 7, 1983, Mr. Fleming announced that ICOD would be incorporated as an international, non-governmental, non-profit organization to assist developing countries in obtaining maximum benefit from their extended zones of maritime jurisdiction through the enhancement of their capacity to develop, manage and utilize the ocean resources off their coasts. The resources of the world's oceans are an obvious source of food, minerals and other things for developing nations. The ability of developing countries to use those resources is uncertain, and this point was brought forward during the 1981 Commonwealth Conference in Melbourne,
Australia, when Prime Minister Trudeau released a statement which announced that it was Canada's intention to create an international centre for ocean development as part of a three-point training program aimed at increasing Third World production. That news release stated that the Centre would focus on research, training and technical co-operation to help poor countries increase food production from the sea and take advantage of new harvesting rights expected to be gained under the Law of the Sea negotiations.
In December, 1983, the Speech from the Throne which opened the second session of the Thirty-Second Parliament included the following statement:
Economic progress is a crucial contributor to peace and stability. Recognizing the urgent needs of developing countries, the Government will maintain its commitment to overseas development aid. Canada will achieve aid goals of 0.5 per cent of the Gross National Product by 1985, and 0.7 per cent of the GNP by the end of this decade. Increased involvement of voluntary organizations and the co-operative movement will be sought in the delivery of this aid. Particular attention will continue to be given to the growing world food crisis, through existing programs, and the new International Centre for Ocean Development.
When Prime Minister Trudeau announced the objectives of ICOD he stated, and I quote:
With an operational budget of approximately $20 million over a period of five years, the International Centre for Ocean Development would seek to help developing countries get optimal return from their recently expanded marine resources with a major focus being the oceans as a source of food.
A lot of work has gone into establishing this new Centre. The previous speaker for the Government outlined some aspects. ICOD classifies the ocean resources in three general categories. We have mentioned living resources, mineral resources and other resources such as ocean energy, transportation, recreation and tourism. They are all very important. Canada has established a reputation in the scientific, technical and managerial aspects of ocean development. Many Canadian training and research centres already have strong links with foreign institutions and international development projects. ICOD was set up to take advantage of this experience and provide a base to complement the work of other national and international organizations involved in ocean development.
Over the years Canada has developed an outstanding program in the provision of food and technology to developing countries. The fisheries industry has become more important over the years, especially with the development of the 200-mile limit which gave maritime developing countries exclusive access to the riches that the ocean environment provides. The world food catch is about 75 million tonnes, of which about 70 per cent or 52.5 million tonnes is consumed by humans. The remainder is reduced to oil or meal for animal feed. So there is a tremendous opportunity for developing countries to take advantage of the resources of the sea.
Canada is not only a major producer and exporter of fish, but it is also one of the most knowledgeable of fishing nations. It is important that our specialists in both the private and public sector share this knowledge with developing nations in order that these countries may manage and use their resources more successfully.
February 14, 1985

ICOD will certainly contribute to international development, as the previous speaker mentioned. But there have been other fisheries-related programs supported through other federal departments. The International Development Research Centre has supported fisheries projects with objectives to reduce waste and expand productivity in the world fishery. In 1983-84, IDRC was allocated $2.5 million in fisheries projects. CIDA was the main channel for Canadian assistance to fisheries projects in developing countries, although other departments have played and are playing a major role in the development of some of the poorer nations, the so-called Third World countries. Non-governmental organizations also play a very important role in fisheries development. With support from the federal Government, these organizations work on projects affecting 28 countries.
Canada also continues to provide direct food aid in the form of salt and canned fish in situations of acute food shortages. That has a very beneficial effect not only on our international relations, but in some cases it has the effect of creating and strengthening the market for fish products within our own country. I think of things such as canned mackerel. That is a very difficult species of fish to process because it arrives in large quantities over a very short period of time. It is therefore very difficult for some of our processing operations to handle these quantities. One of the easiest ways to process mackerel is canning. Therefore, there are times when we have large inventories of canned mackerel, a very good food product, one that is certainly needed by some Third World countries. Over the past number of years we have contributed great amounts of canned mackerel and salt cod, as well as some more expensive fish products.
So, Mr. Speaker, obviously we have a great number of programs aimed at helping Third World countries and therefore I hope that we on this side will see this Bill go through quickly. We have probably one or two more speakers on this side who would like to make some comments on this Bill this afternoon. We hope that the Bill will go through. We would not want to hold it up in any way because we recognize the importance of the Centre. We realize that this legislation must be passed on a timely basis in order to get the funding in place. The Centre is presently operating under the broad wing of CIDA.
It is important that the Centre continue to be located in Halifax. There are several important fishery institutions in that area, such as the Bedford Institution of Oceanography. Dalhousie University has an excellent program in marine biology. In my own riding, we have Holland College in Sum-merside, which is a fisheries related training centre. There are several others in Nova Scotia which contribute in large measure to the research and effort in the fishing industry within the country and in our foreign endeavours. Halifax is a good location for that reason. It is very important that a centre of this magnitude be near such sources of information. It is equally important that these institutions be in close contact
Ocean Development Centre
with the Centre in order to maintain their own international dimensions.
The Halifax location may be a little more expensive than some others. If the Government's commitment of only $3.3 million is an indication of support for the Centre, it may be lost. It is crucial to get more funds for it. The Centre is presently a non profit, non-governmental organization. Because of the great importance of flexibility and quick reaction in times of developmental need, I hope that the change in status to a Crown corporation will not impede the Centre's objective. I am concerned about that. I hope that the Centre will be able to continue to take advantage of other sources of funding as well without reductions in federal funding. It may be able to get contributions from private sources. I would not want those contributions to be substracted from the Government funding. Funding should be maintained to promote growth rather than be impeded or levelled off to the status quo.
I hope that the people who worked so hard to create the Centre can sit back now with pride in their accomplishments, assured that the federal Government will continue to support the Centre in its objective. I was involved with the Centre a year ago. I have always had a personal interest in fisheries-related research projects. I feel that through the Centre Canada can help Third World countries. Many countries simply throw money into foreign aid. I have always been of the view that it is not good enough to simply throw money. You must increase the knowledge and expertise in Third World countries to enable them to continue to provide their own food. Those countries need better education to develop and become as productive as the more affluent countries.
I would like to wish the new Centre well. I hope that it will be run on a scientific basis and that the Government will not influence or destroy it by not getting well qualified people to direct the corporation. I hope the Government will realize that it is important to stay away from the daily operations of the program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak in support of Bill C-22, an Act to establish the International Centre for Ocean Development. The Centre is already in some form of operation. It was inaugurated in 1983 by a decision of the previous Government, a decision which we supported at the time. I would like to speak in approval of the principles of the institution, but I will raise some questions about the trends in development we have been seeing in recent years under the previous Government and, more recently, in recent months under the current Government.
The objectives of the organization are quite obvious.

They are both obvious and praiseworthy. I quote from the Bill: '
The objectives of the Centre are to initiate, encourage and support co-operation between Canada and developing countries in the field of ocean resource development by

February 14, 1985
Ocean Development Centre
(a)	initiating and supporting programs in developing countries for the improved management and utilization of ocean resources, particularly as a source of food;
(b)	supporting the development of indigenous expertise and institutions in developing countries in order to increase the capacities of developing countries in integrated ocean use management;
(c)	enlisting the expertise of people and institutions in Canada, developing countries and elsewhere;

-and furthermore to organize and support the collection of information which would result from these activities and to organize the necessary services in relation to that.
These objectives are fine. Canada does have expertise in oceans and has a contribution to make in development. However, I am concerned that we make this a genuine contribution to development. I noticed that it was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Mclnnes) who introduced this Bill in the House. We need to be a little suspicious of the motives of Canada in having this treated as a trade matter rather than an aid matter. The International Centre for Ocean Development acknowledges that when it stated:
"Canada has been a major beneficiary of the Law of the Sea. Throughout the protracted negotiations, this country has found common cause with developing coastal states and has, in turn, benefitted from their support. As a recognized leader in technology relevant to the oceans and as a donor country whose motives are not open to suspicion by recipients, Canada shares an exclusive niche with few other developed countries.
This is all very nice in theory, but how true is it? We have certainly benefited from the Law of the Sea Conference, the extension of our boundary by 200 miles.
However, the trends in development work on land and in the sea also give us cause for concern. Some countries are becoming quite suspicious of our motives because Canada is increasingly tying its development aid to trade. Canada is supporting large scale, technically advanced development projects opposed to small scale community projects with appropriate technology. These large scale projects essentially turn out to be an expensive export subsidy program for a small group of Canadian industries. Some of these industries are subsidiaries whose profits go to the foreign head office in any event. We fear that the trade emphasis is becoming even more pronounced under the new Conservative Government than it was under the Liberals. Certainly, the trend began under the previous Government and we opposed it then.
Non-development criteria are being tied to development criteria. Specifically, CIDA has imposed a requirement that 80 per cent of all bilateral aid be spent on the purchase of goods and services in Canada and that two-thirds of the value of such merchandise be added in Canada. That is excellent for Canadian business and there is no reason why Canadian businesses should not take advantage of trade opportunities that arise through development work. Obviously there are advantages through genuine expertise as well as economic spinoffs through this type of work.
However, it is completely unfair to tie aid to these requirements to make countries buy from Canada. Those countries may not get the best deal because they could be producing the goods and services locally. This is also preventing them from developing industries from which we could be buying goods and services to help them develop.
This is occurring in spite of our own government studies showing that the tied provision increases the cost of Canadian aid to recipient countries by almost 20 per cent. Those countries are forced to spend one-fifth more for the goods that they require for a particular project. In short, it is costing them money to receive aid from Canada. This policy perpetuates underdevelopment in the Third World while providing an artificial stimulus to Canadian trade.
It is our sincere hope that the International Centre for Ocean Development will not fall prey to the trend that we have already seen in other forms of aid. Canada's non-governmental organizations, which are very active in development, could supply valuable advice and expertise. That non-governmental community strongly supports separating the ties between aid and trade, and has very much endorsed small scale community projects for the benefit of the country in order to promote their independence and productivity and emphasize their objectives.
I also note that the Centre's brochure gives some emphasis to the development of tourism as an industry, which is cause for some concern. If an adequate structure for tourism is not in place, that industry could actually contribute to underdevelopment.
Let me refer to a study conducted by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in 1976 by P. F. Wickenden. It states:
-money spent by tourists can have up to 90 per cent leakage. Most of the tourist dollar goes to foreign owned hotels, food importers, liquor importers and is drained right back out of the country-
This does not lead to development. Therefore, we are somewhat skeptical about tourist development because it is not appropriate for all countries.
I also want to make some observations about the sexist language in the Bill and the sexist bias in the creation of the board of governors, since there will be new directors, I hope their appointment will show some change.
The language of the Bill is sexist. We are approaching April 17, 1985, when women are supposed to become equal with men in Canadian society. However, that is not the case when one reads a Bill or an Act of Parliament. It is time that such Bills contained language which includes women and men.
I do not raise this as purely an academic point. The board of directors has a chairman and a president. All the directors who have been appointed up to now are men. The literature is entirely masculine in its orientation. Yet there are women who are active in fisheries and ocean research. I cannot believe that there are no women qualified to be on this board of directors of the Centre. Half of the new directors to be appointed will be non-Canadians. Let us ensure that a reasonable proportion of
February 14, 1985

those directors, both Canadian and non-Canadian, are women. Women have a contribution to make to development.
Let me point out that at the Copenhagen Conference on Women in 1980, Canada recommended that women be included in decision-making roles in their own Governments, and in international agencies, including the United Nations. Canada, together with women from Third World countries, stressed the importance of the involvement of women themselves in development and in decision-making.
While we espouse this view at international conferences, are we living up to it here? It has not happened yet and I hope the Government will take notice.
With respect to the extent of development aid, my Party has encouraged increased development aid up to 0.7 per cent of GNP per year. We have recommended that this take place now. This figure has been discussed and accepted as an objective, only to be postponed. The cuts in development aid in the last year represented a further step back from this extremely modest goal for international development. The cuts in CIDA and IDRC are absolutely unjustified. I suggest it is rather hypocritical to establish a new institute as an independent agency with a modest $20 million in funding over the next five years while, at the same time, the Government is taking money out of development.
We want to see a genuine improvement in development aid, because there is a great need for such improvement. It is true that Canada has economic problems and high unemployment. However, our economic problems are not as great as those in Third World countries. We cannot use that as an excuse for not being generous at this time. Other countries are suffering enormously and hunger in the world is severe. This new institution provides us with an opportunity to increase food production from the oceans. The Government should not be hypocritical by contributing to this institution on the one hand while cutting back on other aid projects on the other.
While we support the spirit of the institute and its creation, and hope that it will be able to help developing countries become self-sufficient in food production, we do not want this to happen at the expense of other development programs that are already in place.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to spoil what appears to be unanimity among all three political Parties so far as this Bill is concerned. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) who was so instrumental a couple of years ago in getting this particular institution under way in the Province of Nova Scotia, even if it was in Halifax and outside this riding.
I listened to the speeches of Members today. When I looked at the Bill I realized that it talked about improved management and utilization of ocean resources, particularly as a source of food, ocean resource development, and supporting research related to ocean resource development. Also it referred to the fact that the Centre may carry on its activities throughout Canada. Today in the House Hon. Members talked about the great expertise and great knowledge of ocean resources which exist in Canada. When I sat and listened to the debate, I thought about the fishermen and the fish plants which I represent. If we are looking for waste in the oceans or mismanagement of an ocean resource, we need look no further than at Canada itself.
We talk about our great expertise and the fact that we will pass on our expertise to another country. I wonder whether or not in that expertise we would suggest that any country in the world should permit 60 per cent of its capelin to be thrown overboard after it is caught because the only utilization for it is to sell it to the Japanese. In fact, we can only sell female capelin to the Japanese. It is absolute dumping, absolute waste.
In the months of July and August on the East Coast of Canada we see the most incredible dumping of codfish. The excuse is always given that it is the glut season and we must have dumping. If we look at the absolute waste in the herring fishery, we realize that the main utilization of that resource is for bait. In fact, it has been encouraged over the years as bait. An Hon. Member mentioned mackerel. I can tell the House
2370

February 14, 1985
Ocean Development Centre
that we have incredible dumping in the mackerel fishery in the country. I cannot see any end to it. Also I could mention squid. An Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party mentioned women as far as development, resource management and expertise are concerned. There are thousands of women involved in the squid fishery in eastern Canada. There always have been. It was their main source of employment before the Japanese decided not to buy any more dried squid. Of course the resource itself diminished somewhat.
When I look at our resources and our expertise I sometimes wonder why we never implement our own suggestions to developing countries. Also I wonder how long all fish in our oceans can be managed by two separate administrations. One manages them on the land and the other manages them in the water. In other words, everything in the ocean is managed by the federal Government. However, what happens to the fish when they come ashore? They are managed by provincial Governments. That is the way it has always been and that is the way it will always be. This is why we have seen over the years-and we will continue to see it-the Government of Canada having to bail out fish companies.
The reason I say this is that the only utilization of our ocean resource in this country has been by local private enterprise family-related businesses. That is a fact. When we look at the problems in our ocean-related industries, that is problems in our food supply, we see that they were restricted to our exports of fish products going to another nation to be made into a finished product. That is a very interesting statement. It is interesting that those who got into trouble were the people who took the food resource from the ocean and froze it into a gigantic cod block to be exported to the United States or to another country. There it was thawed, an occupation employing thousands of people, and put into the final package. It was then sent back to us as a final product to be placed on our food shelves.
Are we going to suggest that to a developing country in another part of the world? Of course we are not. We in this country are tied into a system of divisions of authority and divisions of regulations. What happens in the fishery does not depend solely on the federal Government. What happens in the fishery and the utilization of a food resource does not depend solely on the provincial Government.
I stated a moment ago that we have one of the most serious problems of any country in the world as far as the fishing resource is concerned. In order to substantiate that, I want to read from A New Direction for Canada, An Agenda for Economic Renewal, put out by the present Government. It reads:
-the major problems lie with over-capacity in the processing sector and low and unstable incomes in the inshore fisheries ... New approaches are required . .. Consolidation of employment in the sector would have to be complemented by public and private initiatives to promote job opportunities in other sectors of the economy, as well as fair and generous adjustment programs for workers in the sector.
I suppose that is the reality of the Canadian fishery today. In effect, what the Government is saying is what every economic expert who has looked at the Canadian fishery has said for years, that is, that workers have to be displaced and that plants have to close. If we were to manage our fishing resource as we are suggesting to foreign nations today it should be managed, there would be no closures and no lay-offs. If we were to utilize the products that come out of the ocean the way that the Soviet Union does, for example, there would be no unemployment in certain regions of this country where there is chronic unemployment today.
It is not good enough in 1984 and 1985 to have massive dumping of fish in this country day after day in the months of July and August. It is not good enough either to say to a full-time fisherman that he can only sell his fish on Tuesday and Thursday to a fish plant on the East Coast of Canada. That is not good enough because the technology utilized in the inshore fishery covers some 20,000 full-time fishermen in this country. What is utilized is commonly called a gill-net. A gill-net drowns and kills the fish on the bottom of the ocean. You cannot leave that fish dead on the bottom of the ocean for three days. What do the fishermen do? They simply have to clean out their nets and throw the fish overboard.
We have systems operating in this country and regulations concerning licences. Even at this very minute there are people fishing for crab 30, 40 or 50 miles off the coast of this country. These people have a stable income. In the spring, the full-time fisherman who fishes groundfish catches crab in his gill-nets. He has to take that over the side of the boat, kill it and throw it overboard because he is not allowed to sell that crab. In the last four or five months, we have seen changes in regulations in restricted licences. We have seen lobster licences, for example, sold to individuals for a price under the table because there was a carte blanche policy initiated by the Government to allow transfers of restricted licences.
When you talk about utilizing an ocean resource, particularly as a source of food, and talk about supporting research related to ocean resource development, go to the small communities in eastern Canada and tell the fisherman that you are going to tell the foreign countries how to do it. He will look up at you, laugh in your face, and say, "That is just too bad because I have to dump my fish in the ocean every single summer".
There is a final point I want to make. There appears to be in this Chamber an attitude toward people who draw unemployment insurance. If that attitude is allowed to prevail as it relates to primary producers who fish the ocean resources of our country, I am afraid that we are going to have half of our inshore fishermen in this country not involved in the fishery in years to come.
We have a basic problem. It involves a system of almost guaranteed income. We have utilized employment opportunities and we have utilized almost a wage subsidy program called unemployment insurance. It was never intended to be a wage subsidy program or a guaranteed annual income, but it is. It is the only one available.
February 14, 1985

Another part of this Bill talks about the employment utilization of the food resource in the ocean. The danger exists in across-the-board changes in the unemployment insurance system proposed by the present Government that will virtually starve the self-employed person who draws unemployment insurance. Some may say that a self-employed person cannot draw unemployment insurance, but that is wrong-fishermen can. I pass that caution to the Government.
When cuts are announced, we must think about the food resources of the ocean as a food supply. When the Government brings in cuts, it must consider how that affects a person who is so important to this economy, who contributes perhaps more than Members of Parliament, lawyers or doctors to the economy of this country, that is, those who utilize the resources of the ocean, our fishermen.
This Bill contains some 100 cases of increases of charges to our primary producers in order to assist foreign nations. There are 100 instances where fishermen will face increased charges. These have to be looked at by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) in the spirit of assisting fishermen. I am referring to all kinds of things, from the increased price of the chart that the fisherman needs to find where he is going, to the little matter of telephoning the weather office and having to pay for it. There is also the cancellation of the fishing vessel insurance program, which will undoubtedly put a lot of fishermen into bankruptcy. I would say that 50 per cent of the fishermen in Newfoundland would be put into bankruptcy. They would lose their boats because it does not match with the regulations made by the provincial Government which has loans outstanding on their vessels.
In conclusion, the reason for my intervention was quite simple. Resources of the ocean are not being utilized in Canada today. Where they are being utilized, they are being underutilized. We are tied into a system in which governments and economists say that we are guilty of low productivity in the sector that relates to a food resource of the ocean. They say that we have a problem of low productivity in the fishing industry, not realizing that you cannot compare apples and oranges. You cannot compare people who half finish a product with people who finish a product, working in the same type of industry in a different country.
They also blame our problem of having no finished product on the tariff rate. They say that Britain has a 10 per cent tariff and the United States has a 7 per cent tariff. These experts, the economists in our country, some of them supported by corporations and organizations of the federal and provincial Governments, have been saying that since the mid-seventies when our dollar was at par with the United States. They have been saying that and they still say it today when there is a 15-cent difference on the dollar and there is only a 10 per cent tariff.
I admire the Government for doing this and I admire the previous Government for instituting this institution. However, it is very difficult for some of us in this Chamber who
Ocean Development Centre
represent poorer sections of the country, for those of us who represent people who are trying to live on unemployment insurance payments averaging $122 a week to support a family, to realize that these people have to dump most of the food products they take out of the ocean every single summer. I apologize to Hon. Members for such an intervention, but I think it is an important one. I think it is an important one for me to make if I am to represent the people who I am supposed to represent.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) has brought to us an astounding revelation. Presumably, in the Hon. Member's mind, the way to help alleviate this problem would be to put fish under one jurisdiction, either federal or provincial. I wonder if the Hon. Member could tell us, in his opinion and possibly the opinion of his Party, which level of Government should take over jurisdiction from the other level of Government.

Mr. Speaker, I will express my own opinion on this matter. I would say that I would not care where the benevolent dictator came from. It is probably a benevolent dictator who would be needed to straighten out the problems in the fishing industry.
Of course, there are also other problems relating to the dual jurisdictions. There is also a problem of attitude and of monetary connections between countries. We also have a problem of attitude in this country. It is interesting to hear the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) question me on this subject because I forgot to mention something that was very dear to his heart, and that is, the absolutely outrageous waste in the Arctic of seals. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, fishermen today are killing seals for the meat and throwing away the pelts.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext: Why? Because they cannot sell the pelts. The pelts are discarded. The meat is kept. I am sure the Hon. Member will agree with me that in most parts of the country, the meat normally sells for about $30 per carcass. In my district, that meat is canned. In my riding, there is an industry that employs 100 people and is canning seal meat right at this very moment. Not very many people know about that. However, the absolute disgrace to those who object to the seal hunt is that the seal pelt is thrown away. That is incredible.

The House resumed from Thursday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bissonnette that Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, I want to wish all of my colleagues on all sides of the House a happy Valentine's Day.
First of all I would like to thank my hon. colleague, our business critic, for giving us a heart, which is something I have never found yet among the Conservatives. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to continue my participation in the debate on this Bill. With respect to the problems that will be generated by a Bill that will increase the cost of loans for people working in small businesses, all Liberal Members have pointed out to the Government that the problem is already with us. Today we have seen that interest rates are rising. We have seen that it is already a problem to find investment capital, and especially for small businesses. What is happening is that the Government is saying it will no longer guarantee 100 per cent of the loans given by Canadian banks. As soon as this Bill is passed, Mr. Speaker, it will become increasingly difficult for small businesses to obtain loans. That I am absolutely sure of.
Anyone who has worked in a small business knows that the two main problems are cash flow and obtaining capital, especially venture capital. I fail to understand why a Government that made so many promises during the election campaign, saying that it would increase assistance to small businesses, reduce the burden of excessive reporting regulations on small
businesses .. . Mr. Speaker, there is a big difference between these promises and what is really happening.
I was shocked when this Bill was introduced, shocked at the fact that the Conservative Government of Canada was not prepared to guarantee the fees to be charged to small businesses. Mr. Speaker, big corporations like Dome Petroleum will always be able to get more capital, whether or not at the expense of small businesses. In fact it will always be at the expense of small businesses. With this new legislation it will be even more difficult for the people who elected this Government and who were promised relief from the excessive regulatory burden on small businesses.

I frankly cannot understand how, in good conscience, this Government, a Government which allegedly promised small business that it would make the load easier, that it would in fact reduce the kind of excessive bureaucracy with which small businesses are faced, would introduced a piece of legislation which will, with certainty, increase the difficulty in borrowing for small businesses and, in particular, small businesses which are entering into the market-place in the high technology fields. They are the ones who are in need of the kind of venture capital which we know is going to be necessary to bring this country into the 1990s. The Government introduces programs like Abandon Canada or Investment Canada, saying, "We will open our doors wide. Canada is not only open for business but it is up for sale". At the same time, it is tightening the screws on private enterprise which has actually made this country run. Because the Government has refused to guarantee to 100 per cent the kinds of loans which are currently being administered by our banks, we are certain there will not be the kind of availability of venture capital which exists even now. Those of us who have worked in small business will know that the situation is already tight.
If the Government, in its naivety, expects that the banks are going to tell small business that they will absorb that 10 per cent differential between what the Government is now prepared to guarantee and what a small business needs to expand and improve its business, it is wrong. If the Government believes that the banks are going to tell the small business people, "No problem. We'll cover you for the 10 per cent", then the Government has no idea of the kind of difficulty which is currently being faced in the money market by the small business sector.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that by introducing this particular Bill, the Government has abandoned its commitment to the small business sector and has abandoned the 300 promises it made. A dozen of these promises related strictly to the small business sector, and we see that this sector, like the widows and senior citizens who happen to be single or divorced, is being abandoned by this Government because its quest for power does not take into account the delivery of the promises it made before September 4.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a very short comment. I have been listening to the debate on this Bill since the Bill
February 14, 1985

was introduced. There seems to be some misunderstanding when the statement is made that the loan should be 100 per cent of the total cost of the project. There is no such federal guarantee. In other words, Mr. Speaker, under all of these programs the person applying for the loan has to put up a certain percentage of the total cost. In certain ventures under the Small Businesses Loans Act, he has to put up 20 per cent, and in other ventures, 10 per cent. There is no such thing as a total 100 per cent. It is 100 per cent of the loan which is given by the bank for the remainder.
The two organizations who appeared before the Finance Committee recently claimed that the fee which is introduced by this legislation should not be imposed on the bank but should be imposed on the individual businessman who is getting the loan. By some strange logic they think that that is the proper way of imposing the fee. The fee would still have to be paid. I would like to ask the Hon. Member what she thinks of imposing the fee-as the Federation of Small Business claims-prior to the loan on the individual who is borrowing and not the bank.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) for his question. He has aptly pointed out the difficulty caused not only by the Government cutting back on its particular commitment to guarantee the loan portion which is not assumed by the borrower, but the difficulty which any business person is going to have when faced with this added increase in cost imposed, whether it be directly to the business person himself or herself or to the banks. I would agree with the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate and disagree with those who would say that the banks should pass along this cost directly to the borrower in the form of an increased surcharge. I think the small businesses of this country have had enough surcharges and they do not need another surcharge.
I would also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the bank is going to be passing along this surcharge, not only to the borrower directly, but also to any others who are doing business on a surcharge basis. Whether the increase is directed specifically to the small business or indirectly through the bank in its own levying charges, the Government is in fact, through another inflationary mechanism, adding to the cost of doing business in this country.
I suspect that the best solution for small business people, and in the interests of keeping the kinds of promises which were made during the election campaign, is for the Government to respond to the criticism from this side of the House by withdrawing the Bill. I was frankly surprised earlier to hear the comments of the members of the third Party who support the Government in saying that it should not have to guarantee to 100 per cent the small business loan portion which is not being assumed by the small business person. From the point of view of the Liberal Party, I disagree absolutely and totally with the position which is being taken by the Conservatives and the New Democratic Party. We believe that small business people have a hard enough time getting venture capital in the first place and they should not be further impeded by the
Income Tax Act
kind of surcharges which were mentioned by the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate, and the other kinds of punitive charges which are currently being considered in this particular Bill.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, in order to eliminate the hardships brought about by previous amendments, which now make workmen's compensation reportable as "income" for Guaranteed Income Supplement purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am taking the liberty of introducing this motion today in the hope that I can count on the assistance of all Members of Parliament regarding the amendments I am seeking. I wish to point out that this situation is having a devastating effect on a great number of Canadians, particularly senior citizens. The situation prior to Bill C-139 being passed in the previous Parliament was that individuals completing applications for the Guaranteed Income Supplement were asked about other forms of income they may have. One form of income which was excluded from reporting at that time was workmen's compensation payments. However, that practice, which was in effect for about 15 or 20 years, was changed under Bill C-139. The contents of that Bill were not readily noticed by Members in this Chamber on either side of the House. In fact, I think it was the labour unions who brought it to our attention. I raised the matter in the previous Parliament to try to seek an amendment. Other Members from other Parties, Conservatives as well as New Democrats, also sought changes. There was some meaningful discussion in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs when Members of Parliament got together and made an oral submission to the then Minister of National Health and Welfare in an attempt to rectify what we believe was a wrong.

February 14, 1985
Income Tax Act
I want to point out very clearly that I fought against that change, as did other Members of Parliament from the Conservative Party and the NDP. I thought we were very close to reaching a decision on changing the law back to the way it was. Well, that is history now. The election came along and most of those Members of Parliament are gone, except for those on the Conservative side.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext: Some went to the other place.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
That is right, some of them did. Quite seriously, Mr. Speaker, the amendments that I seek here today relate to Sections 81, 56 and 110. With those amendments we would have in effect the old legislation back in force. Because of the amendments which went into effect with the passing of Bill C-139, workmen's compensation payments are reportable for purposes of determining the GIS. As a result, senior citizens in Canada are finding a substantial reduction in income. Not only that, in some instances it has disrupted their lives.
Certain provincial Governments have programs available to recipients of the GIS. Now that workmen's compensation payments are included for the purposes of the GIS, there has been a reduction, and indeed some people have lost their GIS. We are not talking about Canadians who are making a lot of money. We are talking about Canadians who live below the poverty line, maybe just on the poverty line or just above it. These people have been in the workforce for a considerable period of time but, through no fault of their own, have received an injury. I might add that the money they receive from workmen's compensation is not 100 per cent of their wages. Not at all. It is something less than 100 per cent. In 99.99 per cent of the cases it is not through choice that these people are on workmen's compensation; it is because they sustained an injury and were unable to return to work, and they are now in their retirement years. This has had a devastating effect on those Canadians who are receiving both the GIS and workmen's compensation because the payments have been lowered.
What has been the extent of those reductions, Mr. Speaker? Has it been much? Well, When you do not earn a lot of money, a reduction of $5 is a lot. For some of my constituents the reduction has been $160 a month, or $58 or $134 or $25 or $191. When you are on a fixed income and energy costs are going through the roof, when the price of food increases-and it does not go down-for a government to come along with legislation to take that benefit away is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is utterly wrong. My Government was wrong. The then Minister of Finance was wrong in putting that legislation through. Well, now we have an opportunity to right that wrong.
I have here a copy of Hansard which shows those other Members of Parliament who agree with me that we ought to change this provision of the Income Tax Act. I hope my friend, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), will say a few words in support of this measure. It is important. The reductions have been susbtantial. It is not as if an individual is making $100,000 a year and you are slicing off $200 a month. That is not the case. The case is that it is less than $10,000 a
year and you are being slashed by $200 a month. It hurts and we ought to change that. God knows, we have made many changes for the rich, so what is wrong with our senior citizens and those hovering around the poverty line receiving an advantage? The bureaucrats will argue that, conceptually, it has to be calculated as income for the purposes of the GIS. I say, shame on the bureaucrats. We in this country have given many tax advantages to the rich and the more fortunate, to various regions of the country, so why can our senior citizens not enjoy a privilege they had for 15 or 20 yeras?
As I said, there is support for this amendment. The former Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence was supportive. The Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) stood in this House on February 22, 1984, to support this change. The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), a Conservative Member, stood in his place on June 1, 1984 and denounced this situation, as I have done, and said he wants it changed. The then Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni, Ted Miller, a New Democrat, supported that amendment because he knew that these people are living from hand to mouth and it is difficult enough in these very turbulent times to get by.
There was support then and it is here today, but what about support outside this Chamber? The Ontario Federation of Labour, The Nova Scotia Federation of Labour and the senior citizens of this country, when they came together in convention, supported this change. The United Mine Workers of America agree that there ought to be a change. The senior citizens clubs in Glace Bay, New Waterford and Reserve Mines agree on this. Mr. Guy Brown, a Liberal MLA in Nova Scotia is supportive of this change. The Nova Scotia MLA for Cape Breton Nova is supportive of this change. He represents the labour party in my riding. There is great support for this in Nova Scotia as well as across the country.
On previous occasions Conservative Members of Parliament have echoed the statements which I am making today. This is not fair or just. It is all well and good to condemn the previous Government, as I did when I was in government. However, that does not help the senior citizens. Members of Parliament must take their responsibility seriously and demonstrate to the Canadian people the will of all Parties to right this wrong. All sorts of bureaucrats can give the legal opinion that conceptually it ought to be reported for the purposes of calculating the Guaranteed Income Supplement. We give advantages to other groups in society. Why can we not restore a benefit to senior citizens in the country?
I am hopeful that Members opposite will take this opportunity to join with me in attempting to have that wrong righted. I am not asking Members of Parliament to be entirely political. However, if they wish to be political and condemn the previous Government, that is fine. However, let us change this provision for the benefit of senior citizens. Canadians across the country want this change. Unfortunately, they do not belong to a national organization which is well-heeled like a
February 14, 1985

chamber of commerce that can come to Ottawa and give articulate presentations and documentations. They do not have that advantage, but they do have Members of Parliament. I believe that it is the duty of a Member of Parliament to represent his constituents. That may sometimes fly in the face of what the Government is attempting to do. I said then and I say now that the Government was wrong to do what it did. Let us change the provision for the benefit of the senior citizens in the country.
There would be no shame for the Government to introduce an amendment. The Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) can do that through a Ways and Means motion. He can change it in the budget, if he wishes.
I sincerely request members of the Conservative Party to amend this Act to enable thousands of senior citizens to have an extra $191 or $25 a month. This is an opportunity for Members of Parliament to ensure that this Parliament is constructive. Surely to God we can bestow upon two million Canadians a benefit which they had for 20 years. Surely the wrong that was committed can be righted. We have the means to do it.
I suggest that there is some political will within this Chamber, Mr. Speaker. I will not mind what is said by Members who rise to speak on this issue. However, I will mind what they do. It is a serious matter when you live at the poverty level and the big hand of government takes a small amount of money away from you. To those individuals it is a significant amount and it hurts. The Prime Minister talked about civility before he entered this Chamber and shortly thereafter. I hope that civility will prevail in this Chamber on this issue. I hope that government Members in particular, as well as those in the New Democratic Party, will support me in this.
The Government will reap benefits if this change is made because people will respond favourably to it. I will applaud the Government for making it. I very sincerely ask all Members of Parliament to change this provision so that workmen's compensation will not be included for the purposes of calculating the Guaranteed Income Supplement.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) has put his arguments forward in such an eloquent and compassionate way that no one who has listened can doubt his sincerity or his very real concern for the people who have been affected by this change. We should all compliment the Member for raising a matter which has caused members of all Parties considerable concern, particularly in the last Parliament. I know from the tone of the Hon. Member's comments that he does not view this in a political manner. He is not making this a partisan issue. He has appealed to us not to make it a partisan issue either, but to put it forward for serious consideration.
My own position on this matter is equally non-partisan. On matters of tax and social policy all Members would prefer to consider things from a non-partisan point of view.
I would like to take this time to express the concern, not only of the Hon. Member but of all Members, for senior citizens throughout Canada who have been affected in a number of ways by various pieces of legislation. I suggest that a review of the situation will explain the purpose of these provisions and why it would be inappropriate at this time to support the Hon. Member's motion. Let me emphasize that I do share the fundamental concern for the welfare of our senior citizens that I know is felt by the Hon. Member.
My concerns about his motion arise from a strong concern of my own about the concept of equity and fairness to all Canadians which must surely underlie all that we do.
As Hon. Members are aware, the Income Tax Act amendments in question were first raised in the Budget presented in November of 1981. I know that the Hon. Member has freely criticized those amendments which were introduced by his Government. I do not think I could match his condemnation of the changes that were introduced in that Budget. None of us who were there at the time can forget that there were a number of other measures included in that Budget which had disastrous effects on other groups of Canadians throughout the country. The question we must ask is whether or not the Hon. Member supported that Budget when it came before the House. I would assume that he supported it and its measures, including the one under discussion today.
If I may refer to documents issued at that time to explain the proposal, it is clear that the amendments were intended to put all similar programs on the same basis with respect to the calculation of eligibility for payments under the Guaranteed Income Supplement and Child Tax Credit provisions.
Specifically, the then Government wanted to deal with cases where some recipients of GIS were already in receipt of substantial income from workmen's compensation, and yet were placed on a par with those who had no other income. It wanted also to clear up a problem in a more general area of

February 14, 1985
Income Tax Act
taxation. Previously, a person claiming the dependant deduction did not have to take into account any income from workmen's compensation which his dependant might have. But would it be right to allow eligibility as a full dependant someone in receipt of as much as $20,000 in some cases?
It is important to note that the change proposed was implemented in such a way as not to affect an individual's tax payable, as it was recognized that such a change would indeed mean hardship for a number of those receiving workmen's compensation and other payments.
Let me also emphasize a very important point with respect to this issue. The changes did not alter the special status of workmen's compensation payments, whereby they are not subject to tax themselves. We are talking about the effect of including income which is already granted special treatment.
In 1984, a number of Hon. Members, including the Hon. Member from Cape Breton, raised the matter in the House when it became clear that one effect of the change was to reduce GIS payments for certain persons. The matter was also raised by some columnists in the press. The Hon. Member also pointed out comments made by other individuals. In the debate on Bill C-40 in the second session of the last Parliament, both in the House and in the standing committee, the issue was thoroughly considered.
The committee consideration of the question now being raised was most interesting and the basic rules underlying the debate emerged from it with some clarity. One very important point was with respect to the GIS program itself; another related to the Income Tax Act and its approach to the sources from which taxable income is derived. Then there was the question of how workmen's compensation payments are viewed, whether as replacement for income or as payment for the injury itself.
Finally, the testimony of the then Minister of National Health and Welfare pointed to the question of the amount of work needed to deal with the problem, which she admitted had not been anticipated by her or her officials. I think it is worth-while to look at each of these points.
My concern in taking the time to deal with them is that I do not want the House to rush into correcting something that may be regretted by some Members, when hasty action may in fact cause greater problems or raise issues which are best left for more careful study in a more appropriate way. It would be most inappropriate to consider just one small matter without considering how it fits into the general policies being followed by the Government.
Because the motion deals in effect with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, I would first like to consider that program. It is important to remember that the GIS is a program directed to the poorest of our senior citizens, those whose income would otherwise consist solely of payments from the Old Age Security program and possibly small amounts of other income. It is addressed to those people who are not able to provide for themselves in their later years and who would otherwise be left in a very depressed state economically.
Because the Government does not want to penalize those who have small additional income, there is a threshold below which benefits are not reduced by added income. Above that threshold, GIS entitlement decreases gradually by 50 cents for every dollar of income until benefits are completely eliminated. Surely this demonstrates that the GIS is not and never was intended to be anything other than a program directed to low income members of our society. Even the requirement that persons in receipt of the GIS must apply each year is evidence that the authors of the program recognized that changing circumstances might raise an individual's income and so reduce the need for the GIS.
Let me take a moment to point out that in the current year, the threshold above which GIS is not paid is over $11,000 for a single person and over $16,500 for a couple. Obviously, those at this level are not well off and they have my sympathy and that of the Government. But there are many who are worse off. Should we be considering a change which would put those in receipt of workmen's compensation benefits in a superior position to those who have no income other than OAS and GIS?
Another important principle which comes into play in this debate is one of the basic foundations of the Income Tax Act. This Act attempts to deal with all income and to treat it fairly across the whole range of sources. No one is going to claim that the Act is perfect and that there are no possible improvements. However, we ought to be careful before we support a move which may reduce the equity of certain provisions of the Act.
It would be difficult to argue that some sources of income, such as workmen's compensation payments, should be treated differently from other types of compensation. This was the situation prior to the 1981 Budget. Other disability payments have always had to be declared as income for the purpose of eligibility under the GIS, and it is not clear why workmen's compensation ought to be different.
I know that it is urged that compensation payments are different in kind from most other sources of income. Some view them exclusively as compensation for injury in the sense that a cane is some measure of compensation for an injured leg. Surely, however, workmen's compensation is not that, at least not that in its main thrust.
Many members of the standing committee made it clear last June that they accept that workmen's compensation payments are intended to replace in whole or in part the income which an individual would otherwise have earned and on which that person would of course be liable to pay tax or to be assessed for the purpose of GIS eligibility. The fact that compensation payments vary in duration as well as in amount reflects the fact that the awarding boards realize that income replacement during a period of deprivation is a significant function. How can we state categorically that compensation payments are different in kind from other types of payment when they are not viewed as being different in kind by the very bodies which decide on their duration and amount?
February 14, 1985

I recognize with the Hon. Member who moved this motion that individuals who may have received deductions in GIS payments unexpectedly were, not unreasonably, unhappy when that happened. Equally however, I must look at the broader picture in which some people who receive quite large incomes from workmen's compensation awards, such as up to $20,000 as I noted earlier, would still have been in receipt of the entire GIS payments. I do not think that those people whose only source of income is the OAS and GIS would view as fair changes to allow some other people with substantial other sources of income to be placed on the same basis as themselves.
We should also take note of the comments of the then Minister of National Health and Welfare who told the standing committee in June of 1984 that she and the then Minister of Finance decided that to take any positive action in response to the Members' concerns would not be appropriate. They saw clearly that the implications of undertaking this action would be very far-reaching.
The current Minister of a National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has announced that his officials are carrying out a comprehensive review of which sources of income should be included for GIS purposes. This-and I think this is a very major point in my response-is an appropriate way to consider the type of proposal which the Hon. Member has made in his proposal, namely, that the Government is looking at this issue very seriously and that changes may be made, but those changes should be done in the context of the entire review and not on a piece-meal basis.
An additional complication, which might result from an ill-judged amendment along the lines of the motion before us today, concerns the implications for the provinces. Hon. Members may be aware that prior to the changes we have been discussing today, it was necessary to pass remission orders every year to ensure that certain maintenance payments made by provincial Governments were not to be viewed as income for the purposes of GIS eligibility. The changes made in the 1981 Budget in this area ensured that there was a greater uniformity of treatment for all similar payments, whether federal or provincial in origin, and did away with the necessity for repeated remission orders. Again, however, I do not want to seem to be unfeeling toward those who were affected adversely by this measure. But I have to take into account that any legislation, and perhaps especially the Income Tax Act, has to deal as much as possible with general provisions.
I take special note here of the Member's comment regarding the bureaucratic mind-set. I think that is an interesting point that has evolved over a number of years and has been shown to be unfortunate in a number of cases. It is one of the things of which I and other Members on this side are mindful and to which we pay significant attention. On the other hand, I do not want to denigrate the activities and the necessity for proper political direction for a proper response.
Income Tax Act
From one point of view it would be nice to have an Act which could be applied specifically to every individual's situation-but such an Act would be many times as long as the present one. Surely we are coming to realize that what is needed is not more complication but less, so that basic equity can be preserved as easily as possible and as few persons as possible see fairness denied by an Act which is too complicated to understand or administer equitably.
We have to take certain facts into account as well when we are considering what action it is appropriate for us to take in response to this motion. It calls for certain actions to be taken by this House to respond to what I think we would all recognize is a difficult situation for some Canadians. The amount of money involved is probably not large when compared with the current level of spending on the GIS program. This level of spending is $2.5 billion a year. I am informed, however, that although 39,000 Canadians over 65 are currently in receipt of workmen's compensation payments, all but about 2,000 of these people are considered to have 60 per cent or less disability and only about 800 are permanently and totally disabled and receiving the maximum amount. We are therefore not talking about a lot of money, but we are also therefore not talking about a problem which, on the broad scale, is as large as many others we face today.
We should remember that the people affected adversely by the sections of the Income Tax Act before us do in fact have as much income as many others, or more. Like other disabled persons they continue to have access to other provisions of the Income Tax Act, such as those which assist the disabled and other programs which recognize the special needs of the disabled in general. Finally, I would point out that even within the group of 39,000 persons who receive workmen's compensation payments and are over 65, many if not the large majority are in any case disqualified from receiving the GIS, as other pensions and personal revenue raise their income levels to above the threshold.
Let me return in closing to the comments which I made at the outset of my remarks this afternoon. I hope that I have made clear that my own feelings about the motion before us are not based on simple partisan politics. I know that the Hon. Member who moved the motion raised this question in the last Parliament and in different political circumstances than today's. I appreciate that Members from both sides of this Chamber agree that the problem he raises is one that is real for those affected and that does not need to be viewed in a purely partisan way.
I hope I have also made it clear that it is not a matter of seeing a need and responding to it in a simple way. There are questions of equity under the law which are raised by it. Do those who support this motion really intend that this one source of income should be set apart and not considered in the administration of one of our major social programs? For it must be remembered that although this motion refers to changing certain provisions of the Income Tax Act, and therefore raises the question of equity and fairness under that Act, the program which is affected is the Guaranteed Income

February 14, 1985
Income Tax Act
Supplement. The mechanism which has been suggested as a means of dealing with a specific situation involves general issues of taxation and income under one Act, but the meat of the question, the substantive issue, is one which underlies the GIS program and our approach to those citizens who have little else to support them.
I think no one can doubt the sincerity, the honesty and the real concern that the Hon. Member who put forward this motion has expressed. I know all Members are interested in this subject. It is not easy, even if there is only one Canadian affected, to see a reduction in income, particularly when that income is seen to be necessary for that Canadian. We are looking at it in a broad context, and I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare are open to changes which are constructive and progressive. I hope that in the future the Hon. Member will be able to support them.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in the debate on this motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Gurbin) has said, no one can doubt his sincerity. He comes from a place and represents a riding that is very much like my own, predominantly a mining community. He really speaks with sincerity and sensitivity about the problems which his constituents are facing because those are exactly the same sort of problems that my constituents face with respect to GIS and having to declare workmen's compensation payments as income.
I think a red herring was drawn across the path of the debate. I do not know anyone in my riding who collects $20,000 a year in workmen's compensation payments. The word compensate means an indemnity. It means "to make up for", and invariably, in 99.99 per cent of cases, in all of the cases, to collect workmen's compensation one has to incur an injury on the job. Oftentimes it is a disabling injury which limits the ability of the individual to earn income to support himself and his family in some dignity. The compensation payment is not only a replacement for potential income, but it is a recognition that there is a handicap. From my experience, the disability results in an incapacitation and a handicap, and there is a cost involved in maintaining the person who is on workmen's compensation. To turn around and say the workmen's compensation payment has to be declared as income seems to me to fly in the face of any sort of fairness.
It was never used prior to the change in Bill C-139. I am really impressed with the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond who correctly castigated the former Liberal Government, his Government, for its chintzy and cheap approach to the Guaranteed Income Supplement. I know he did it publicly, in committee and through letters to the former Minister of National Health and Welfare, Monique Begin.
The argument I heard from the government side is that there is a fairness. The reverse argument is that other people receiving GIS will look at someone who is on workmen's compensation and receiving GIS and say that that is not fair. I
am quite sure the person on workmen's compensation would prefer not to receive any workmen's compensation payments; I am sure he would prefer to be healthy, to pursue his career and to receive an income from his labour. I am sure a person on workmen's compensation would much prefer that than to have an accident and go through the strenuous procedure to obtain workmen's compensation. Indeed, in Ontario, it is one of the most serious problems faced by workers with injuries on the job. The whole question of establishing that the injury took place on the job and the extent of the injury has created a jurisdictional jungle. To argue that a poor person on GIS would look to someone on GIS and receiving workmen's compensation and say that it was not fair, is to reduce the income of the person on workmen's compensation to the lowest common denominator. Instead of saying that we should raise the supplement for the poor person, they are saying that we should knock down the person from the other end of the scale or bring him down to the lowest common denominator. It seems to me that that is inequitable and unfair.
There is another question which I think bears some elucidation. As a matter of fact, it was debated in a committee of the House in the last Parliament. It was debated before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs of the Thirty-second Parliament in 1984. The exact date was Thursday, June 7, 1984. The former Minister of National Health and Welfare, Monique Begin, was the witness. I often see buck passing going on, and we saw it with Monique Begin. She passed the buck to the former Minister of Finance. We must remember that health and welfare came under her jurisdiction. However, in response to the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), she said:
There is an equity problem behind it. That is not easy to face. I understand very well the way the reasoning was made to me. I have it-I do not know through how many letters from Dave Dingwall himself, for example, and from members of other parties-that any additional benefit for a good cause, a disability, a special situation, is something we should protect and should not treat equally with other incomes. Right now the Canadian income tax system has never been made like that.
She concluded by saying:
In a way, that should be discussed with the Minister of Finance, not with me. I am not the Minister in charge of that, period.
The Minister of Health said that that was not her problem, that is was the problem of the then Minister of Finance. Nevertheless, it was made without enough debate or discussion of the matter. Now the Government of the day says that it would like to change it, but that it cannot just make changes because it might create an inequitable situation. Then it talks about the $20,000 per year person who is on workmen's compensation payments, it could be compared to the case of the bank president who makes $500,000 and therefore should not get family allowance. There are only 15 bank presidents in the country. I do not know if there are 15 people on workmen's compensation who collect $20,000 a year.
February 14, 1985

Also the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the previous Government is reported to have said in a debate in the House of Commons:
-that to ignore income from sources such as workmen's compensation would result in inequitably higher benefits for pensioners who have such sources of income than for pensioners without such sources.
Again we hear the argument of inequitability. How can we talk about inequitability when we are talking about couples earning $16,000 per year or about single persons earning $11,000 per year? How can we talk about inequitability in giving them a few hundred more dollars per year? This is something I do not understand.
In the last Parliament the special committee on the handicapped made no less than 11 recommendations with respect to recognizing that a person on a Fixed income with a disability has certain additional expenses which able-bodied persons on fixed incomes do not have. In fact, workmen's compensation payments beyond age 65 become very important in terms of assisting disabled persons to live with some dignity the rest of their days.
The motion of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond is quite appropriate. It seems to me that we can make a change. The Hon. Member said that we were not talking about a lot of money. In fact, it is a lot of money for people living in areas such as Cape Breton and Nickel Belt. When they finally come to fill out application forms-and it is a means test-they have to declare workmen's compensation payments.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment has said that they do not pay any income tax on workmen's compensation payments. That is in fact the way it was worked out. They only receive 50, 60 or 70 per cent of their wages. This is because of the fact that there is no tax on it. If they received 100 per cent, of course they would pay income tax.
We on this side of the House in the New Democratic Party support the motion of the Hon. Member. We urge the Government to correct the mistake of the previous Liberal Government. I know that many Members on the government side in the last Parliament argued against removing this particular provision. I suggest that they should now come out of the closet and stand with us and urge the Minister to return to the way it was before.
