speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really happy to have been able to second the motion of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). I have had many years of experience; in fact one of the first things which brought me into politics was the question of injured workers in the Province of Ontario. When I came to the federal House I was asked by a reporter what was the one thing I would like to do in my term in Parliament. I said that one concrete thing I would like to do would be to assist in encouraging the Government to effect a change to the Income Tax Act, specifically as it related to the punitive measures taken in the previous Budget against injured workers.
Income Tax Act
Although I was not a Member of the federal House at the time I became aware of the discriminatory provisions with respect to injured workers in the Budget of 1983, I immediately contacted the then Minister of Finance as well as the then Minister of National Health and Welfare in order to put on the record my objection and the objection of my constituents to a particular piece of legislation which, while claiming to bring equity into the system, was extremely punitive toward those in our society who can least afford it.
I should like to trace a few misconceptions on the part of some Members who have spoken to the Bill, that is, the notion that somehow compensation should be considered as any other income. If we trace the history of the introduction of compensation in provinces across the country, we will know that compensation in the workplace was introduced in an effort to improve or speed-up the process faced by a worker injured on the job and in an effort to introduce an over-all scheme to cover workers. Each worker in the country has given up his or her right to sue for a safe workplace.
We see from the litigation that occurs in the United States that not many companies will want to revert to the system that we had prior to the introduction of workmen's compensation in the 1930s where each individual was forced to take his or her company to task in a direct lawsuit when it dealt with a case of injury on the job. They gave up the right to sue, which in the 1980s could result in settlements of literally thousands if not millions of dollars.
In my constituency, a worker was blinded while in the employ of Westinghouse. As a result of that incident, he will remain disabled for the rest of his life. That person does not have the right to sue. He will receive a full disability from the Workmen's Compensation Board. He has had great difficulty and a change in his life as a young man as a result of that incident. This points to the need for compensation to be more than simply a retirement or pension plan scheme.
Compensation is more than that. It recognizes the fact that the workers have given up the right to sue. It recognizes the difficulty-I am really sorry if the Members of the Government are not interested in this issue. It happens to be an issue about which I feel strongly. I am sure many hundreds if not thousands of their constituents are concerned about it.
When you talk about injured workers, you are talking about many people whose income is less than $10,000 a year. These people are living below the poverty line, according to Senate statistics and any other statistics that have been furnished. These people are not living in the lap of luxury.
When the amendment was introduced into the Income Tax Act, it further punished workers who had already been deprived of the right to a quality of life which was similar to what they had experienced before their injury. By one stroke of the income tax pen, those workers not only lost their dignity and the quality of life, which had already suffered as a result of their injuries, but they were being further punished financially. I do not believe that the equity argument is being

February 14, 1985
Income Tax Act
compromised in the amendment suggested by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. If the Government sees fit to introduce this amendment, it will receive the full support of all Members of the House. It certainly speaks to the very reasons that we are here in Parliament. As the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond said so aptly, in many respects we are here to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves.
The Government spokesman suggests that most people who are on workmen's compensation are being compensated for only 20, 30 or 40 per cent. I have seen literally thousands of workers who demonstrated before the Legislature of Ontario. Those same workers-

That is the level to which they have been reduced as a result of work injuries and a lack or responsiveness of the Government in recognizing that when an iron worker breaks his arm, he is not 5, 10 or 15 per cent disabled, as suggested by the current compensation system of the Province of Ontario, but is totally disabled.

-I am convinced that if the Government decides to support the Bill as proposed by the Hon. Member whom I have the honour of supporting myself because if there is one thing I can accomplish during my four or five years here in Parliament it will be to change this provision to have a little more justice for our workers and a little more dignity, and to restore some of the quality of life a worker loses when he or she is hurt on the job. It is a major problem for our workers, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that Members on all sides of the House will support this Bill.
I would like to go on speaking to this proposal, but since we only have five minutes left, I would like to have a chance to vote on the Bill because it is so very important for all Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy indeed to have the opportunity to speak to this motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). I am also pleased to see so many of my colleagues across the way with their shiny noses and smiling faces. I am sure they have paid a good deal of attention to this debate because, as the Hon. Member said, it is an important debate. I agree very much with the contents of this motion.
All Parties in this House have shown their interest in this amendment. In the last several years, they have supported many changes in the Old Age Security Act. They are very concerned with the financial needs of pensioners. Special attention has been given in this House and by my Government to income-tested benefits provided under the Act because we all recognize that these benefits have been targeted to those who need help the most.
My Government has moved in this direction by moving the spousal allowance down to ages 60 to 64. That Bill is now before the committee. My Government recognizes that we are dealing with limited resources. The idea in the 1950, 1960s and 1970s that there was no limit to the amount of money that we could provide has now disappeared. There is not a nation in the western industrialized world that has not had to either cut back on social benefits or to increase the contributions of those who receive the benefits. The demands for education and medical care have to be offset by the demands for pensions.
My Government recognizes that the great question in the 1980s is to ensure that we achieve a rational pension system which will ensure that no one retires without sufficient means to lead a decent life. In that sense, pensions have to be targeted. I believe everyone recognizes that.
The previous Government introduced a measure which has caused a great deal of difficulty for one group of Canadians. That, of course, is the subject of the motion before us today. It was an amendment to the Income Tax Act which was passed during 1983. It made the compensation benefits of workers accountable as income, but not subject to tax.
The main effect of that change, which received some publicity at the time and some opposition from Members on all sides of the House, is that the recipients of the GIS, spousal allowance and OAS had to begin declaring any workmen's compensation benefits as income. In some cases this reduced or eliminated supplements for many pensioners. That is a good example of bringing in quick changes in legislation without assessing the side effect it may have on other legislation and other programs. That is the reason why my Government is examining the whole question very carefully and cannot go along with this isolated change.
The Minister in charge will do a complete review of how income for GIS recipients will be assessed and what has to be done in this regard. This is an important issue which the Hon. Member has raised. It is a valid concern. Members may have had as much concern about the way it was done as about the actual change itself. Workmen's compensation is now counted for the purpose of income tax. I am sure that in the future, we will see some changes in this area and that we might see many changes. I note that it is now six o'clock. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
February 14, 1985

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-SUSPENSION OF CALGARY CABLE STATION
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-SUSPENSION OF CALGARY CABLE STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 14 last, based on the decision of the CRTC to disallow a Christian program heard in Calgary and surrounding area, I asked the Acting Minister of Communications in the House of Commons on December 14, 1984, if the Minister would look into the said suspension and ascertain why the CRTC is so opposed to Christian programs and Christian music. The Acting Minister, the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean), took the question as notice and advised the House that he would personally raise this matter with the Minister as he had a special interest in the subject.
On January 16, 1985,1 received a reply to a letter I had sent to the CRTC in which I deplored the said suspension. This letter indicated that the Christian program that had been suspended would now be allowed. So the people won and the program may once again be heard in Calgary and area.
The second part of my question about the reason why the CRTC is so opposed to Christian programs and Christian music, has gone unanswered so far. 1 am very concerned about the attitude and the actions of the CRTC regarding Christian programs and Christian music. Let us look at how the CRTC handled an application made by Canadian Family Radio Limited of Vancouver.
At the original hearing in October, 1978, the CRTC questioned the applicant extensively on its religious program with the proposed concept of family programming. The CRTC was informed that like other applicants, the proposed station was a commercial venture totally dependent on its revenue from the sale of advertising and thus would have to appeal to a broad audience and that no religious group or organization would control the station.
In February, 1979, nine commissioners of the CRTC gave unanimous approval in principle to the application. However, four months later the CRTC changed its mind and called a second hearing which was held on February 12, 1980. The applicant was then kept waiting for five more months even
Adjournment Debate
though the Commission had knowledge of the mounting financial outlay of the applicant.
On July 9, 1980, a full 15 months after nine members of the CRTC had given the application unanimous approval in principle, the CRTC denied the application. The CRTC considered that there was too much religious content. Has the CRTC become a censor board?
I should mention that some commissioners of the CRTC did submit a minority report, part of which stated emphatically that the conditions that the CRTC had imposed on the applicant could not reasonably be met. Again, during the second hearing four months after nine commissioners of the CRTC had given approval in principle, the CRTC pulled a fast one by having six members present, two of whom were new, while five members who were on the panel when the approval was given were not in attendance. Even with this substantial change, there was still a minority report. The CRTC's handling of this application destroyed a lot of its credibility and, in my view, the Canadian Family Radio people were treated shabbily. That is why I ask why the CRTC is so opposed to Christian programs and Christian music. The CRTC was so determined to reject this application that even when the applicant finally offered to comply with whatever the CRTC required, the CRTC simply ignored the offer.
Time will not permit an exhaustive review of legislation, but I must refer to Section 3 of the Broadcasting Act which clearly states that all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for programs they broadcast but that the right to freedom of expression and the right of persons to receive programs, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations, is unquestioned.
Furthermore, the CRTC's anti-Christian and anti-religious policy infringes on Sections 1 (c) and 1 (d) of the Canadian Bill of Rights which recognize freedom of religion and freedom of speech, and Sections 2(a) and 2(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which guarantee the freedom of conscience and religion and freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including of the press and other media of information.
In the United States there is no bar to Christian or religious programs. If the people like what they hear, they listen and support the station. If they do not want to listen they turn it off, and the company will not stay in business very long if there is no support for the station. But in Canada, at least until now, the people have no such choice. An appointed board says in effect, "We will not license a station that specializes in Christian programs and Christian music". How much longer will the people tolerate this bureaucratic discrimination that is contrary to the Broadcasting Act and contrary to the Canadian Bill of Rights and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION-SUSPENSION OF CALGARY CABLE STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for

February 14, 1985
Adjournment Debate
his very persuasive comments. I know that he was pleased to learn that the CRTC took action on December 21, 1984, in Public Notice 1984-318, in which it indicated it is now prepared to allow the continued carriage of religious U.S. FM stations.
The CRTC's non-renewal of the Calgary cable system's authority to carry U.S. religious radio station KMBI as a cable audio service had been the result of a policy announced by the Commission in May, 1984 that it would not renew existing authorities for the carriage of U.S. religious radio stations. This had an impact on cable systems across Canada and in British Columbia, Alberta and Kingston, Ontario, in particular. Both the Department of Communications and the CRTC received numerous complaints from cable subscribers who found themselves suddenly deprived of U.S. Christian radio stations which they had, until then, been able to receive on their cable audio service. But as I have said at the outset of my remarks, this situation has now been corrected and the continued carriage of religious U.S. FM stations will be allowed.
I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to point out that the CRTC has also approved the concept of a Canadian national interfaith religious television programming service delivered by satellite to cable systems. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, an application from the Canadian Interfaith Network to provide such a service is currently with the Commission.
This application from the network was received in response to an invitation from the CRTC to all interested parties to file applications to provide a predominantly Canadian interfaith religious programming service that would be varied and comprehensive, reflecting equitably the religious practices and beliefs of Canadians. It would be delivered by satellite to cable systems across Canada. The CRTC also asked applicants to give consideration to the manner in which regional or local religious programming might be included to supplement the over-all program schedule of the national service.
The Canadian Interfaith Network, CIN, or Reseau Inter-Religieux Canadien as it is known in our other official language, was the only organization to submit an application in response to the CRTC's call, but it represents several religious groups in Canada. At a public hearing on November 27, 1984, the network appeared before the CRTC to report progress on the development of its membership structure and on other questions related to its application. Speaking at that hearing, as a representative of the network, the Hon. David MacDonald noted:
It is fundamentally important for the commission to realize that the network is not merely a collection of individuals with an interest in religious broadcasting. Rather, it is an entity which has grown out of a time consuming and difficult process of due consideration by the governing bodies of the various religious communities, amounting to a direct and formal commitment by these bodies. This fact, in itself, sets the network apart from any application the commission has ever received-or is likely to see again.
The Hon. Member will know that our former colleague, the Hon. David MacDonald, is a former and distinguished Minister of Communications. He is a man of the cloth and a man
who knows full well the importance of interfaith and religious broadcasting.

subtopic: POLITICAL PARTIES-TORONTO ELECTION CAMPAIGNS- STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF FINANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR APOLOGY
POLITICAL PARTIES-TORONTO ELECTION CAMPAIGNS- STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF FINANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR APOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate this evening and specifically to readdress the question I asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on December 14. I had referred to some statements that were made in a Canadian Press interview with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He was quoted as saying that, "The election campaigns we fight in downtown Toronto are 'don't vote for the Tories or they are going to send you back to Italy. That is what is at the door. That is the politics that people will play. It is the politics of fear'."
At that time, Mr. Speaker, I and many others from the Italian community, in fact Canadians from different communities, took offence at those statements. When I asked the question of the Prime Minister and followed it up in correspondence, it was sad to see the patronizing attitude taken by the Right Hon. Prime Minister. I will quote part of his answer:
-I thank my hon. friend for his observation. For my part and that of my Party, we have been honoured by the support that we have received from the Italian community in Canada-
There are two things wrong with that. First, it is a patronizing, off-base attitude which did not address or acknowledge the statements made by his Minister of Finance. Second, the statement is not true. They did not get support from the Canadian-Italian community. If one looks at the electoral statistics, one will quickly realize that is not the case.
These statements are wrong, Mr. Speaker, and derogatory for two essential reasons. First, he is saying that my Party, including myself, as well as the NDP, fought a campaign in Toronto based on fear. He is saying we went to the doors of Canadians of Italian extraction and said that if they do not vote for us but vote for the Tories, they are going to be sent back to Italy. That was not the case, Mr. Speaker. Neither I nor any member of my Party conducted that sort of campaign.
I challenge the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to come forward with evidence to justify those very serious allegations. They should not make those statements without bringing forward proof. If they do make them, as they did, they should be prepared to retract them and apologize for the shortsightedness of the statements.
The second thing wrong with that statement is that if those two other political Parties conducted such campaigns, which they did not, the Minister of Finance attributes low intelligence to Canadians of Italian background. It is interesting to see that in that same interview the Minister of Finance said that Canadians are not given credit for their intelligence on the issue of social programs. He then finished his interview with the derogatory statement I read into the record earlier. Is the Minister suggesting there are two types of Canadians? Perhaps there are, on the one hand, Canadians who do under-
February 14, 1985

stand the system and the mechanisms, and, on the other hand, those new Canadians who are more gullible. Well, that is not the case either, and that was perhaps the greater offence.
This is a community that has come and worked here and it understands and appreciates the Canadian political spectrum. They participate in the Canadian mainstream and the political process. They also come from a country which gave us Machiavelli, so I do not think we have to be lectured by any Minister of the Crown to the effect that one particular Canadian community is gullible enough to believe that if you vote for the Tories the political fall-out will be deportation.
We live in 1985, Mr. Speaker, and I thought those kinds of comments were passe. Obviously they are not, and so I sought from the Prime Minister an acknowledgement that the statements were erroneous, uncalled for, and that he should send the right signals to those communities to the effect that they are a well respected part of this country. I believe that the injustice that has been done is that the Minister and the Prime Minister have failed to grasp the opportunity to send those signals to those communities and to admit that those statements were in fact unfortunate and unsubstantiated.
In subsequent press articles, the Minister of Finance said that he saw no reason to retract those statements. The Prime Minister answered the letter by saying that the Italian community gave them even greater support in the last election. That is the type of patronizing attitude that will not instil a sense of confidence in the communities of new Canadians. It will not instil a sense of confidence in the promises and commitments that he and his Government made to the multicultural communities of the country and to the multicultural policy. If we are to give credit and weight to these commitments and promises, the statements made by the Minister of Finance should be taken off the record. It should be admitted that they were a mistake. If those statements go uncorrected, members of the Italian Canadian community will not look to the Government with such grace. I hope we will receive a correction and retraction of those statements in the answer given by the Parliamentary Secretary this evening. I am looking forward to hearing from the Hon. Member at this time.

subtopic: POLITICAL PARTIES-TORONTO ELECTION CAMPAIGNS- STATEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO MINISTER OF FINANCE. (B) REQUEST FOR APOLOGY
speechtext:
Signor Presidente, sone honorata di rispondere a nomme del mio collega l'onorevole Michael Wilson. I am very pleased to be here responding to this question because I am angered by the opportunism which has been shown by the Hon. Member opposite. I am very proud that in my riding there are 7,000 Italo-Canadians. That is not patronizing, Mr. Speaker. Those people are my friends, as are people from the German, Anglo, French and Hungarian communities in my riding. Some of the warmest memories I have of the campaign are of visiting with people in the Italian community in my riding, many of whom were my friends before I ran for public office and have been welcomed in my home. I resent the implication that the Hon. Member has left in his remarks throughout this discussion that somehow this is patronizing.
Adjournment Debate
The very second stamp in the first passport I ever had as a Canadian was from Italy. I spent a month in the birthplace of western culture. I have been back and intend to return again, because Italian Canadians are among the people who I am proud to call my friends. I do not regard it patronizing to say so, and neither do they.
I would like to point out to the House that our Party is committed to representing all communities in Canada. I would like to emphasize that the Party of Mazankowski, Hnatyshyn, Della Noce, Jelinek and Mitges objects strongly to such allegations. Canada's cultural communities voted in overwhelming numbers for this Party on September 4.1 see no reason that we should not be proud of that. This is a record of which we are proud and a record on which we will build in the future.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has also stated:
I want to be able to say that our country is one where all citizens have an equal opportunity to achieve their full potential; a society which strives for equality in all aspsects of life, where people applaud ingenuity and daring and reward creativity and excellence.
I am very proud to belong to a Party which stands for that kind of philosophy. I am only sorry that the Hon. Member opposite has chosen to use this as an opportunistic political topic.

Mr. Speaker, the occasion for my speaking this evening in the House is as a result of a question that I put to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) some weeks ago. It was with regard to whether he would favourably consider a proposal by the Maritime Farmers Council to enhance the Feed Freight Assistance Program which has been in place since 1941 to assist farmers in feeding their livestock and being competitive in the market-place.
In 1984 the agricultural community recorded record bankruptcies. Approximately 551 farmers went bankrupt. When the Minister was addressing the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, he stated that the Government had to pay attention to the 39,000 farmers who are in severe to moderate financial distress but who have a chance to survive. A substantial number of those farmers, plus a number who went bankrupt in 1984, and a substantial number who will go bankrupt if the Government does not take positive action, live and make their living in the maritime provinces.
They are facing this crisis because they are not competitive and cannot obtain a decent return for the fruit of their labours. Many of them are not competitive because of the differential in the feed grain price between the maritime provinces and western Canada, Ontario and Quebec.
The feather industry in the maritime provinces is in trouble. It currently pays a differential in excess of $60 per tonne for feed grains that are imported into the Maritimes to raise their stock. The dairy industry has seen a decrease in the amount of fluid milk demand as a result of $47 and more per tonne that it

February 14, 1985
Adjournment Debate
must pay in excess of its brothers in Ontario, Quebec and western Canada. The beef industry is also in trouble.
The pork industry is in serious trouble because of the excess $37 it must pay per feed grain tonne to import it to the maritime provinces.
In 1941, the Feed Freight Assistance Program was brought into effect by the Government of the day. At that time it covered approximately 90 per cent of the cost of transportation of grain from the Lakehead to eastern Canada. Over the years that price eroded to the point where, between 1967 and 1976, it was approximately 59.3 per cent of the total cost of transportation.
Today, farmers are being compensated to the tune of approximately 19 per cent to 28 per cent for the importation of Ontario corn and 26 per cent to 33 per cent for western grain. Our farmers cannot bear that type of depletion in their incomes.
For example, the hog producers in Ontario are receiving approximately $13.99 per market hog sold, plus an average payment of $4.90 covered under the Agriculture Stabilization Act. The average return of a market hog sold is $18.89. His brother in the maritime provinces is receiving a net farm income per hog sold of 14 cents, compared to the $18.89.
What we are looking for in the maritime provinces is the ultimate goal of self-sufficiency in the production of feed grains. In the meantime, only 45 per cent of that land available to us is under production. We have the potential for substantially more land production, but it is going to take a few years to get it into production. There is a plan in place. We expect by the year 2000, if that plan is implemented, that we can be self-sufficient in the maritime provinces. In the meantime, we ask the Government to do what it has done for Canadian farmers in the West, what it has done for the Crow rate, and what it has done through the Stabilization Act for farmers here in Ontario and Quebec, to provide farmers in the maritime provinces with only what it is providing for those other farmers in the rest of Canada, that is, the same type of assistance. What it amounts to is an immediate infusion of $13.3 million in new money which would be added to the $7.2 million already identified as dollars that would be injected into the Feed Freight Assistance Program, for a total of $20.5 million. As our agricultural land is put into production to make us self-sufficient in the growth of grain products, the amount will reduce each year, naturally. As more land comes into production, the more self-sufficient we become, the amount will lessen, and by the yeawr 2000 it will have been eliminated.
The key words are short-term. It is for the short-term period. The food and agricultural sector in the maritime provinces is vital to our economy and to our survival.
I ask this Government to approach this serious plight positively. The nearly bankrupt farmers in the maritime provinces are dependent upon feed grain importation. I ask the Government to give them every serious consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his representation on a very serious topic, one about which he is extremely concerned and one on which I know he has worked hard in the past and will do so again in the future.
I would say at the outset that this Government is committed to the survival and prosperity of the livestock and poultry industry throughout Canada. In the case of the Maritimes, we believe that the long-run prosperity of the livestock and poultry industry would be well served by increased local feed production. Indeed, the Maritime Farmers' Council has stressed this very point. To that end, two actions have been taken.
First, under the agreements with the provincial Governments, about $74 million will be spent on agricultural development over five years. Part of this money will be spent on research to develop improved varieties and cultural practices suited to the maritime conditions. Part may also be spent on improving the dissemination of information aimed at improving grain producers' efficiency and also on improving the grain marketing structure.
Second, locally produced grain was made eligible for feed freight assistance payments. This was done to ensure that maritime grain producers were not disadvantaged by the feed freight assistance payments made to assist local livestock and poultry producers.
Feed freight assistance is of course an important means of ensuring the competitive position of the maritime livestock and poultry sector. In 1983-1984, $4.8 million was paid on shipments to the Maritimes. Moreover, in the last 10 years the proportion of feed freight assistance expenditures paid for shipment in the Maritimes has increased from 17 per cent to 30 per cent.
As the Hon. Member has indicated, the Maritime Farmers' Council has proposed increasing feed freight assistance payments to cover 50 per cent of transportation costs from western and central Canada. As my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) indicated in the House of Commons on December 18, 1984, we would, of course, be willing to consider the merits of this proposal. I would, however, add a note of caution. Given the difficult budgetary position we have inherited from the previous Government, it would be necessary to identify financial resources which could be used for such a project.
